q: Your agent must verify identity (get_customer) before process_refund. A teammate adds “Always verify the customer before issuing refunds” to the system prompt, but in testing it still skips verification ~3% of the time on refund requests. What is the most effective fix?

choices.t: Rewrite the verification rule in emphatic, capitalized MUST language and move it to the very top of the system prompt.
Add a programmatic gate in the loop that refuses process_refund until get_customer has returned a verified customer ID.
Add an evaluation suite that replays recorded refund transcripts and fails the build whenever verification was skipped.
Add three few-shot examples showing verification before a refund, covering the phrasings that produced the misses.

exp: Ordering that must hold on every run belongs in code: a gate cannot be talked out of blocking the call. The evaluation suite is the strongest alternative and will catch a regression before release, but it reports on refunds that already ran instead of stopping one. Emphatic wording and more examples both stay probabilistic.

q: process_refund can fail because the payments service is briefly down, because the amount exceeds the customer's eligible total (policy), or because the caller lacks permission. Today every failure returns “Operation failed.” Which tool-side change best lets the agent respond correctly to all three?

choices.t: Return structured error metadata: a category (transient/validation/business/permission), a retryable flag, and a readable explanation.
Retry the transient payments-service failures inside the tool with backoff, and surface only the failures that survive the retries.
Return the upstream exception message and HTTP status code unchanged, so the agent can interpret the underlying cause itself.
Retry any failed refund up to five times with exponential backoff before surfacing anything at all to the agent.

exp: Three failure classes need three different responses, so the tool must name the class instead of leaving the agent to infer it: a category plus a retryable flag says retry, explain, or escalate. Retrying inside the tool is the strongest alternative — right when a flaky dependency is the only failure mode — but here it handles one class and leaves the other two indistinguishable. Raw exception text classifies nothing.

q: A customer opens with “I want to talk to a human, now.” The underlying issue — a duplicate charge — is something your agent could resolve in a single call. What is the most appropriate first action?

choices.t: Escalate immediately with a structured handoff naming the duplicate charge you identified and the fix you would have applied.
Resolve the duplicate charge first, since it is one call, then hand over to a human with the refund already completed.
Acknowledge the request, then ask two quick diagnostic questions so the handoff summary carries verified account context.
Route the message through sentiment scoring and escalate only once the measured frustration crosses the configured threshold.

exp: An explicit request for a human is honored as stated; the agent's remaining value is the quality of the handoff, not overriding the request. Resolving the charge first is the strongest alternative and would be right had the customer not asked — here it substitutes the agent's judgment for an explicit instruction. Diagnostics add friction, and sentiment scores something the customer already said outright.

q: Across a long multi-issue conversation, the agent starts restating exact figures (refund amounts, order numbers) vaguely and occasionally wrong. Which technique best preserves these facts?

choices.t: Extract transactional facts into a persistent case-facts block included in every prompt and kept outside the summarized history.
Summarize the conversation more aggressively each turn so the exact figures stay inside a smaller, more focused context.
Raise max_tokens on each response so the model has room to carry the full history of figures into the next turn.
Ask the customer to re-state the order number and refund amount whenever the agent is not certain of a figure.

exp: Progressive summarization is what turns exact figures into vague prose, so the fix keeps them out of the summary: a case-facts block re-states them verbatim every turn. Summarizing harder compounds the loss, a larger output budget does not restore what was already condensed, and re-asking moves the burden onto the customer.

q: A message says: “My order #882 arrived damaged, I was double-charged on #877, and I want to update my shipping address.” All three are within the agent's capability. What is the best handling pattern?

choices.t: Decompose the message into three items, investigate each against the shared customer context, then reply once with all three resolutions.
Resolve the two order issues now and open a separate tracked ticket for the address change, telling the customer where it went.
Work the three items strictly in sequence, re-verifying the customer at the start of each so every branch stands alone.
Ask the customer which of the three matters most, handle that one, and offer to cover the rest in a follow-up message.

exp: All three are in scope, so the agent decomposes, investigates against one verified customer context, and resolves them together in a single reply. Splitting out the address change is the strongest alternative and is right when an item needs a different team — here it makes the customer track two threads for work this agent can already do. Re-verifying per branch wastes calls.

q: To “future-proof” the support agent, a colleague wants to give it all 18 backend tools (inventory, marketing, analytics, HR…) even though the workflow needs about 4. Why is this risky?

choices.t: Selection reliability drops as the catalog grows, since every extra description is another candidate the model must rule out.
The cost is the extra tool-definition tokens on every request; selection accuracy itself holds steady as the catalog grows.
The real exposure is reaching sensitive backend systems, which renaming the tools to opaque identifiers is enough to contain.
Unused tools stay inert as long as names are unique, so the workflow keeps working and only the context budget grows.

exp: Over-provisioning measurably degrades tool selection: the model must discriminate among eighteen candidates instead of four, so least-privilege scoping to the role's tools is the fix. The token-cost answer is half right — cost does rise — but it misses the reliability failure, and reliability is what produces wrong actions.

q: Policy: refunds over $500 require manager approval, and you need a guarantee — not best effort. What is the right Agent SDK mechanism?

choices.t: A tool-call interception hook that blocks process_refund when the amount exceeds $500 and redirects into the escalation workflow.
A PostToolUse hook that records every refund over $500 after it runs, so violations surface in the next audit report.
A system-prompt rule stating that refunds above $500 must obtain manager approval before process_refund is ever called.
A few-shot example showing a $600 refund being escalated to a manager rather than processed directly by the agent.

exp: A guarantee means the call is stopped before it executes, which is what interception does. The PostToolUse audit is the closest alternative and is the right instrument for detecting drift over time, but it fires after the money has already moved. A prompt rule and an example both leave the decision to the model.

q: get_customer returns two customers named “Maria Silva” with different account IDs, and the pending request is a refund. What should the agent do next?

choices.t: Ask the customer for one more identifier — email, order number, or ZIP — and act only once exactly one account matches.
Proceed on the account whose recent order history matches the issue described, treating that as a confident single match.
Escalate to a human, since two customers sharing a name is a data-quality problem support tooling should not resolve alone.
Continue with the higher-value account, since a refund posted against the larger balance is the easier one to reverse later.

exp: A refund is irreversible enough that acting on the wrong account is the expensive error, so the agent asks for one more identifier before touching anything. Matching on recent order history is the strongest alternative and is often right — but it is still an inference the customer can settle in one question. Escalating is disproportionate, and picking by balance optimizes for cleanup rather than correctness.

q: The agent frequently calls get_customer for order questions and lookup_order for account questions. Both descriptions are one line (“Retrieves customer information” / “Retrieves order details”) and accept similar identifiers. What is the most effective first step?

choices.t: Merge the two tools into a single lookup_entity tool that internally decides whether to hit the customer or the order backend.
Add a deterministic keyword router that inspects each message and pre-selects get_customer or lookup_order before the turn runs.
Expand each tool's description with input formats, example queries, edge cases, and explicit use-this-vs-the-other boundaries.
Add eight few-shot examples of correct routing to the system prompt so the model learns when to use each lookup tool.

exp: Tool descriptions are the primary mechanism the model uses to choose tools; minimal descriptions are the root cause. Expanding them is the low-effort, high-leverage first step. Merging is a bigger architectural change, a router bypasses the model's understanding, and examples add tokens without fixing the descriptions.

q: In your agentic loop, how should you decide whether to keep executing tools or to stop?

choices.t: Continue looping while stop_reason is tool_use, and terminate the loop once stop_reason comes back as end_turn.
Stop when the assistant's text contains a completion phrase such as done or finished, and keep looping otherwise.
Stop after a fixed cap of five iterations, treating that cap as the loop's primary termination condition.
Stop as soon as any tool returns an empty result, treating the empty payload as the model's completion signal.

exp: Loop control reads stop_reason: tool_use means another tool call is pending, end_turn means the turn is finished. Parsing prose for completion words, using an iteration cap as the primary stop, or reading an empty tool result as completion all guess at a signal the API already reports directly.

q: Your agentic loop calls get_customer, then lookup_order. Before issuing the next model request, what must the loop do with each tool result to keep the turn coherent?

choices.t: Append each tool result to the conversation history in full, so the next model call can reason over everything found so far.
Append a one-sentence summary of each tool result, keeping the history compact across a long multi-tool turn.
Append only the most recent tool result, since the earlier ones are superseded by whatever the latest call returned.
Write each tool result to a scratchpad file and append the path, letting the model read it back when it needs detail.

exp: The API is stateless, so whatever the next turn must reason over has to be in the message list — the full result, not a pointer to it. Summarizing each result is the strongest alternative and is a real technique on very long runs, but it decides what matters before the model has seen it. Keeping only the latest result breaks multi-step reasoning, and an unread file path is not context.

q: Task: add a single null-check to one validation function, with a stack trace already pointing at the exact line. Which approach fits best?

choices.t: Execute directly: the change is a single line in one file, and the stack trace already identifies exactly where it goes.
Open plan mode first and write the change up, since a written plan is cheap insurance on any edit to validation logic.
Execute directly, but run a repo-wide Explore pass first to map every other validation function that may need the check.
Open plan mode and fork the session, so two competing null-check implementations can be compared before either is applied.

exp: Plan mode earns its cost when the approach is uncertain, the blast radius is wide, or several designs compete. Here the fault is located and the fix is one line. Planning first is the strongest alternative and is never wrong in the abstract — it just buys nothing when there is only one way to add a null check. Exploring and forking scale that overhead further.

q: A new teammate clones the repo but doesn't get the team coding standards that everyone else's Claude follows. The standards live in the senior dev's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. What's the diagnosis?

choices.t: User-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is personal and unversioned; move the standards to a project CLAUDE.md so clones pick them up.
The teammate needs an @import in their own home-directory CLAUDE.md pointing at the shared standards file.
The standards load only once the teammate runs /compact, which pulls the synced team memory files into the session.
CLAUDE.md files load only in plan mode, so the teammate has to enable it before the shared standards take effect.

exp: Anything in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md lives on one machine and never travels through version control, so shared standards belong at project level where a clone picks them up automatically. A home-directory import still depends on every developer setting it up, and neither /compact nor plan mode governs which memory files load.

q: You want a /standup slash command available to everyone on the repo after they pull. Where should the command file live?

choices.t: In .claude/commands/ inside the repo, where the file is version-controlled and reaches everyone on the next pull.
In ~/.claude/commands/ on each developer's machine, so every teammate has /standup available locally.
In the root CLAUDE.md under a Commands heading, so it loads for every developer working in the repo.
In a commands array inside .claude/config.json, so the repo declares /standup for everyone who checks it out.

exp: Project-scoped commands live in .claude/commands/ and ship with the repository. The per-developer directory is personal and would need every teammate to add the file themselves, CLAUDE.md carries context rather than command definitions, and there is no commands array in a config file.

q: During a long refactor, Claude begins giving inconsistent answers and referencing “typical patterns” instead of the specific classes it discovered earlier. Best mitigation?

choices.t: Have the agent persist its key findings to a scratchpad file it can re-read, and run /compact to trim the verbose history.
Restart the session and re-explore the codebase, so the discovered classes are re-established in fresh, uncluttered context.
Raise max_tokens on every request so older discovered context is retained and the answers stop drifting between turns.
Ask the same question a few times and keep whichever answer about the discovered classes comes back most consistently.

exp: Long sessions degrade as verbose history crowds out the specifics, so the fix externalizes the findings and compacts what remains. Restarting is the strongest alternative and does clear the noise — but it also discards the discovery you already paid for, which the scratchpad preserves. A larger output budget does not restore what has already been crowded out.

q: Your prose description of a code transformation keeps producing inconsistent results across files. What most effectively communicates the transformation itself?

choices.t: Provide two or three concrete input/output examples that demonstrate exactly what the transformation should produce.
Define a JSON schema for the result and validate every iteration against it, so non-conforming output is caught.
Rewrite the prose description at greater length, spelling out each rule of the transformation and its exceptions.
Lower the temperature to 0 and resend the same description so it is interpreted identically on every file.

exp: Examples pin down a mapping that prose leaves open to interpretation: they show the exact before and after rather than describing it. Schema validation is the strongest alternative and is worth having — but it checks the shape of the output, not whether the transformation logic was the one you meant, so a consistently wrong result still passes. Longer prose does not resolve the ambiguity.

q: A multi-phase task keeps exhausting context because the discovery phase dumps verbose file listings into the main conversation. Which change contains the cost without losing the discovery?

choices.t: Run the discovery in an Explore subagent, so only its concise summary comes back into the main thread.
Run the discovery inline but trim each listing to the paths that matched, dropping the surrounding metadata.
Move to a model with a larger context window and keep the discovery inline, so the listings stop exhausting the budget.
Write the discovered listings into CLAUDE.md, so they are available on every turn without being regenerated.

exp: A subagent gives discovery its own context window and returns only the conclusion, so the verbose middle never enters the main thread at all. Trimming the listings is the strongest alternative and is right when you control the tool output — it reduces the volume but still accumulates in the main conversation. A larger window raises the ceiling without containing the growth.

q: A review surfaces several issues. Two of them interact (fixing one changes how the other should be fixed); the rest are independent. How should you communicate the fixes?

choices.t: Send the two interacting issues together in one message, and handle the independent ones separately.
Send all of the issues in one message and let the fixes be worked out together, saving a round-trip on each.
Send each issue in its own message in severity order, so every fix is applied and verified in isolation.
Send the issues in one message without saying which two interact, letting the model infer the dependency itself.

exp: Fixes that change each other belong in the same message so the model can account for both; independent ones lose nothing by being separate. Batching everything is the strongest alternative and is fine when nothing interacts — here it buries the one dependency that matters. Splitting them all apart breaks the pair, and withholding which two interact hides what the model needs.

q: You return to an investigation a week later, and the files you analyzed have changed substantially since. What is the soundest way to continue?

choices.t: Start fresh with a written summary of the earlier conclusions, since the cached tool results no longer describe the files.
Resume the session but open by telling it which files changed, so it knows which of its earlier results to distrust.
Resume the session as it stands, since a week of accumulated analysis is worth more than re-deriving it from nothing.
Fork the session so the original stays intact, then continue in the fork with the earlier tool results still loaded.

exp: The cached tool results describe files that no longer exist in that form, and stale context misleads more quietly than missing context does. A fresh start with a summary keeps the conclusions and drops the stale evidence. Resuming with a note about what changed is the strongest alternative and is reasonable when a file or two moved — across a substantial refactor it leaves a large body of wrong detail in play.

q: For the topic “impact of automation on healthcare,” reports cover only hospital robotics, missing nursing, diagnostics, administration, and telehealth. The coordinator's logs show it created three robotics-flavored subtasks. What does that evidence point to?

choices.t: The coordinator decomposed the topic too narrowly; each subagent then executed the scope it was actually given.
The web search agent's queries were too shallow to surface sources outside robotics for its assigned subtask.
The synthesis agent dropped the uncovered areas instead of flagging that four subtopics had no findings behind them.
The document analysis agent discarded sources that were not specifically about hospital robotics before scoring them.

exp: The logs are the decisive evidence: three robotics-flavored subtasks means the missing areas were never assigned, so no downstream agent could have covered them. Shallow queries are the strongest alternative and would produce thin results — but thin within the robotics scope, not four absent subtopics. Synthesis and analysis can only work with what they are handed.

q: The synthesis subagent produces reports omitting details the search and analysis agents clearly found, and you have confirmed those agents returned good results to the coordinator. What is the most likely cause?

choices.t: Subagents do not inherit the parent's context, so the synthesis prompt has to carry the prior findings explicitly.
The coordinator is passing a condensed summary of the findings rather than the findings themselves, losing detail.
The synthesis agent is spawned before the other two return, so it composes from whatever has arrived by then.
The findings exceed what one synthesis prompt can hold, so the earliest agent's results are truncated on the way in.

exp: Subagent context is isolated: whatever the coordinator does not put in the Task prompt, synthesis never sees. Passing a condensed summary is the strongest alternative and produces the same symptom — but it is a variant of the same root cause rather than a different one. A race or a truncation would drop findings unevenly rather than systematically.

q: To research three independent subtopics faster, how should the coordinator spawn the subagents?

choices.t: Emit several Task tool calls in a single coordinator response, so the subagents run concurrently.
Spawn one subagent per coordinator turn, finishing each subtopic before the next one is started.
Put all three subtopics into one subagent's prompt and let it work through them in sequence.
Fork the coordinator session three times so each fork researches one of the independent subtopics.

exp: Parallelism comes from emitting several Task calls in one response; the coordinator then waits once instead of three times. One spawn per turn is correct but serial, a single subagent handling all three removes the concurrency entirely, and forking duplicates the coordinator rather than delegating to it.

q: The coordinator runs the full pipeline (search → analyze → synthesize → report) even for trivial queries answerable from a single source, spending time and tokens. Which design change addresses that?

choices.t: Have the coordinator assess each query and select which subagents to invoke, so trivial ones skip the stages they do not need.
Add a fast path that answers single-source queries directly and routes everything else through the existing pipeline.
Keep the full pipeline but cap each subagent's token budget, so a trivial query costs proportionally less to run.
Replace it with a shorter fixed pipeline applied uniformly, trading depth on complex queries for speed on trivial ones.

exp: The pipeline is fixed where the work is variable, so the coordinator has to decide per query which stages the question actually needs. A dedicated fast path is the strongest alternative and handles the case described — but it hard-codes one branch, so the next query shape that fits neither lane needs another. Token caps limit the waste without removing it.

q: The synthesis agent sometimes runs its own web searches and does them poorly. Your data shows 85% of its verification needs are simple fact-checks (dates, names, statistics) and 15% need deeper investigation. What is the best scoping?

choices.t: Give synthesis a scoped verify_fact tool for the common case, and route deeper investigations back through the coordinator.
Give synthesis the full web-search toolset but add prompt guidance on when to hand the harder verifications back.
Have the search agent verify every claim before synthesis begins, so synthesis needs no verification tool at all.
Have the coordinator run all verification centrally, so synthesis receives only claims that have been checked.

exp: Least privilege matches the tool to the role's real need: a narrow verify_fact covers 85% of cases without handing synthesis a browsing toolset it uses badly. Full access plus guidance is the strongest alternative and is simpler to wire — but it leaves the capability that caused the problem in place and relies on the prompt to keep it unused.

q: The web search subagent times out. How should that failure flow back to the coordinator to best enable recovery?

choices.t: Return structured error context: the failure type, the attempted query, any partial results, and viable alternatives.
Return a generic search-unavailable status once the subagent's own internal retries have been exhausted.
Return an empty result set marked as a successful search, so the coordinator continues without special handling.
Propagate the raw timeout to a top-level handler that ends the research run and reports the failure upward.

exp: Structured context lets the coordinator choose between retrying, substituting a source, and proceeding with partial coverage. A generic status is the strongest alternative and does at least signal failure, but it discards the partial results and the query, so every recovery path has to start again from nothing.

q: Two equally credible sources report different market-size figures for the same year, and both are relevant to the report. How should the synthesis output handle the disagreement?

choices.t: Keep both values with source attribution and annotate the conflict, so the reader sees the disagreement and its provenance.
Report the figure from the larger, better-known source and note in a footnote that another credible estimate exists.
Average the two figures and report the blended number, so the reader has a single value to work from.
Report the more recent of the two figures, treating recency as the tie-breaker between two credible sources.

exp: Two credible sources disagreeing is itself a finding, so the report surfaces both with attribution rather than resolving it silently. Leading with one and footnoting the other is the strongest alternative and is reasonable when the sources are clearly ranked — here they are equally credible, so the choice would be the synthesizer's rather than the evidence's. Averaging invents a figure no source reported.

q: A subagent's summary compresses findings into prose and loses which source supported which claim; later, two stats look contradictory but were actually collected in different years. Which two practices prevent both problems?

choices.t: Require structured claim-to-source mappings through synthesis, and require a date on each finding in the output schema.
Have each subagent cite its sources in prose and note the collection year in the body of its summary text.
Merge the sources into one shared citation list and date the report as a whole rather than each finding.
Increase the summary length so provenance and dates survive compression, and ask the agents to be careful with sources.

exp: Both failures are structural: provenance and dates survive only if the schema requires them as fields, so summarization cannot quietly drop them. Prose citations are the strongest alternative and carry the same information — but prose is exactly what compression flattens, which is how the mapping was lost to begin with.

q: A search subagent returns “no results.” The coordinator can't tell whether the search failed or genuinely found nothing. How should subagents report this?

choices.t: Distinguish an access failure that may warrant a retry from a valid empty result with genuinely zero matches.
Return one status for both and let the coordinator judge from the surrounding context which case occurred.
Treat every no-results response as a failure and have the subagent retry the query before reporting back.
Treat every no-results response as a successful empty search and continue to the next stage of the pipeline.

exp: The two cases call for opposite responses — retry one, accept the other — so the report must tell them apart. A single status pushes the guess onto the coordinator, and defaulting either way is wrong half the time: always retrying burns calls on topics that genuinely have no sources, always accepting loses coverage to a broken endpoint.

q: The coordinator receives synthesis output with thin coverage on one subtopic, and the deadline still allows more work. Which orchestration pattern handles this best?

choices.t: Detect the gap, re-delegate targeted queries for that subtopic, and re-invoke synthesis once the new findings arrive.
Re-run the whole pipeline with the decomposition adjusted so the thin subtopic is split into two narrower subtasks.
Accept the output and annotate the subtopic as thinly covered, leaving the gap visible to the reader of the report.
Ask the report agent to expand the thin section from general background so that section reads as complete.

exp: Iterative refinement targets exactly what is missing: detect the gap, re-delegate that slice, re-synthesize. Re-running the pipeline with a better decomposition is the strongest alternative and would work — but it redoes the subtopics that already came back well for the sake of the one that did not. Annotating is right only once time has run out.

q: Your coordinator can't spawn subagents at all. What's the most likely configuration cause?

choices.t: The coordinator's allowedTools does not include Task, which is the tool that actually invokes a subagent.
Each subagent needs its own API key configured before the coordinator is permitted to invoke it.
The fork_session capability is disabled, and that is what the coordinator uses to create its subagents.
The coordinator is running in plan mode, which holds back any action that would spawn another agent.

exp: Spawning a subagent is a Task tool call, so the coordinator must have Task in its allowedTools. Subagents inherit credentials rather than needing their own, forking duplicates a session rather than delegating, and plan mode governs edits rather than delegation.

q: You need to find every caller of a function named processPayment across a large codebase. Which built-in tool fits best?

choices.t: Grep, which searches inside file contents for a pattern such as a function name across the whole codebase.
Glob, which matches file paths by name and extension pattern, returning candidate files to open.
Read, opening each file you suspect and scanning its contents for the function name in turn.
Bash with a recursive directory listing, then choosing which paths look likely to contain the calls.

exp: Finding callers means matching text inside files, which is what Grep does. Glob and a directory listing enumerate paths without reading them, and opening files one at a time does not scale across a large codebase.

q: You want to locate all test files matching **/*.test.tsx regardless of directory. Which tool?

choices.t: Glob, which matches files by path pattern such as name and extension, regardless of which directory they sit in.
Grep, which searches the text inside files for a pattern rather than matching the paths themselves.
Read, which loads the full contents of one file whose location you already know in advance.
Edit, which applies a targeted modification inside a single file whose location you already know.

exp: Glob matches path patterns, which is exactly what **/*.test.tsx is. Grep searches contents rather than paths, Read loads one known file, and Edit modifies one — none of them discover files by name across unknown directories.

q: Edit fails because the anchor text you targeted appears several times in the file, so it is not unique. What is the correct fix?

choices.t: Extend the anchor with enough surrounding lines that it matches exactly one location, then reissue the Edit.
Read the whole file and Write the fully modified version back, replacing the targeted section along the way.
Reissue the same Edit with the identical anchor, since the failure is a transient mismatch on the first attempt.
Run a Bash sed substitution in place, patching every occurrence of the anchor text in a single command.

exp: Edit needs an anchor that identifies one location, so the fix is to widen it with surrounding context until it does — or use replace_all when every occurrence genuinely should change. Read-then-Write is the strongest alternative and does work, but it rewrites a whole file to change a few lines. Reissuing the same anchor repeats the failure.

q: The team wants a shared MCP server (e.g., GitHub) available to everyone, with its token supplied via environment variable and never committed. How should it be configured?

choices.t: In project-scoped .mcp.json, referencing the token through environment-variable expansion such as ${GITHUB_TOKEN}.
In project-scoped .mcp.json with the token written out literally, so every teammate gets a working server on clone.
In each developer's personal ~/.claude.json, with the literal token supplied separately on every machine.
As a documented setup block in CLAUDE.md describing the server command and the token it expects to find.

exp: Shared tooling belongs in the version-controlled .mcp.json, and env-var expansion keeps the secret out of the repository while everyone still gets the same configuration. A literal token in that file commits the credential, the user-level file is not shared at all, and CLAUDE.md is context rather than configuration.

q: The agent keeps reaching for built-in Grep instead of an MCP code-intelligence tool that would answer the question better. What is the most likely fix?

choices.t: Enrich the MCP tool's description so its capabilities and output are clear enough for the model to prefer it.
Add a system-prompt line naming the MCP tool as the preferred option for code-structure questions.
Remove Grep from the agent's allowed tools, so the MCP tool is the only search capability that remains.
Move the MCP server from project .mcp.json into ~/.claude.json so that it loads earlier in the session.

exp: The model chooses tools from their descriptions, so a thin description on the better tool is the usual cause. A prompt line naming the preference is the strongest alternative and often works — but it is a standing instruction competing with the description the model reads at selection time, so it weakens as the catalog grows. Removing Grep gives up a genuinely useful tool.

q: An engineer must understand an unfamiliar legacy module before changing it, and the discovery output is verbose. You delegate the exploration to a subagent — what should it return to the main session?

choices.t: A concise summary of the module's structure and the entry points relevant to the change, not the files it read.
A summary plus the full text of the two or three files the change will touch, so the edit can begin at once.
The complete set of files it opened, so the main session can re-read anything the summary may have omitted.
A list of the file paths it found relevant, which the main session then reads itself before making the change.

exp: The point of delegating discovery is that the verbose middle stays in the subagent's context and only the conclusion returns. Sending the summary plus the few files the edit will touch is the strongest alternative and is pragmatic — but it starts reimporting the volume you delegated to avoid, and which files matter is not settled until the change is designed.

q: What's the most efficient way to build understanding of a large, unfamiliar codebase?

choices.t: Grep for the entry points, then Read those files and follow their imports to trace the flows that matter.
Read every file in the repository up front, so that nothing relevant is missed before the work begins.
Glob every file and read them in alphabetical order, covering the tree in a predictable sequence.
Ask Claude to summarize the repository from its name and directory layout before opening any file.

exp: Incremental exploration spends context on the code that turns out to matter: find the entry points, read those, follow the imports. Reading everything up front pays the full cost before knowing what is relevant, alphabetical order ignores structure, and a summary from names alone is a guess.

q: You are designing an MCP server for your issue tracker. The agent needs to browse the catalog of open issues, and it also needs to close one. How should the two be exposed?

choices.t: The issue catalog as a resource the agent reads for context, and closing an issue as a tool that performs the action.
Both as tools, one read-only and one that mutates, so the agent reaches everything through a single mechanism.
Both as resources, with closing modeled as a write to the same issue resource the agent already reads from.
The catalog as a tool the agent calls per query, and closing an issue as a resource it writes the new status into.

exp: Resources are read-only context the agent consults without taking an action; tools do things that have effects. A browsable catalog is the former, closing an issue is the latter. Modeling both as tools is the strongest alternative and does work — it just spends a tool slot and a call on data the agent could simply read.

q: Task: “Add comprehensive tests to this legacy codebase.” Which decomposition strategy fits best?

choices.t: Map the structure, identify the high-impact areas, then build a prioritized plan that adapts as you learn.
Apply one fixed sequential pipeline to every file in turn, so coverage advances at a predictable rate.
Send a single request asking for tests across the whole codebase and review whatever comes back.
Work through the files in dependency order, writing one test per file until the codebase is covered.

exp: An open-ended task on unfamiliar code calls for adaptive decomposition: survey first, prioritize by impact, then re-plan as the picture sharpens. A fixed pipeline suits predictable multi-aspect work rather than exploration, one giant request has no prioritization at all, and dependency order treats every file as equally worth testing.

q: Your CI job runs `claude "Review this PR for security issues"` and hangs, waiting for interactive input. What's the correct fix?

choices.t: Add the -p (--print) flag, which processes the prompt, prints the result, and exits without an interactive session.
Redirect stdin from /dev/null so the prompt receives an immediate EOF and the command stops blocking on input.
Add --output-format json, which makes the run machine-readable and therefore non-interactive by design.
Set CI=true in the job environment, which most command-line tools read as a signal to disable prompting.

exp: -p is the flag that runs Claude Code as a one-shot command: prompt in, result out, process exits. Redirecting stdin is the strongest alternative and often unblocks a hung command, but it works by starving an interactive session rather than never starting one. --output-format shapes the output, and CI=true is a convention this CLI does not key off.

q: Your CI step runs Claude Code with --output-format json and gets back structured findings. The job must fail the build when a critical issue is present. How should the step decide?

choices.t: Parse the structured findings for the severity field and set the step's exit status from what it finds there.
Treat any non-empty findings array as a failure, since a clean review returns nothing at all to act on.
Have the prompt instruct Claude to exit non-zero whenever it reports a critical finding in its output.
Search the printed output for the word critical and fail the step whenever that string is present.

exp: Structured output exists so a script can branch on fields rather than prose, and severity is the field carrying that decision. Failing on any non-empty findings is the strongest alternative and is a defensible policy — it just blocks merges on advisory findings too, which is what erodes trust. The model does not control the process exit status.

q: Developers ignore your review bot because it flags trivial style nits alongside real bugs, drowning the ones that matter. Which change most effectively restores the signal?

choices.t: Define explicit categories for what to report and what to skip, so nits are excluded by rule rather than by judgment.
Have the model rate each finding's severity and post only what exceeds a threshold you set for the repository.
Instruct the model to report only issues it is highly confident about, so marginal observations are left out.
Post the nits as a collapsed summary at the end, keeping them available without interleaving them with bugs.

exp: The bot has no definition of what counts as reportable, so it reports everything it notices; naming the categories to include and exclude fixes that boundary directly. Severity thresholds are the strongest alternative and do cut volume — but the model grades against the same missing definition, so the threshold moves between runs. Confidence is a different axis from importance.

q: The same Claude session that generated the code is asked to review it, and it rarely finds its own bugs. What explains that, and what works better?

choices.t: The session carries the reasoning that produced the code, so review belongs in a separate instance without it.
The session treats its own output as settled, so review should follow a compaction that drops that reasoning.
The session lacks a review rubric, so the same instance should review again against explicit acceptance criteria.
The session optimizes for agreement, so the same instance should review three times and report repeated findings.

exp: Self-review is weak because the justifications that produced the code are still in context and get re-applied to judging it; a fresh instance simply does not hold them. Compacting first is the strongest alternative and attacks the same cause — but compaction summarizes rather than removes, so those conclusions survive in condensed form. A rubric leaves the bias untouched.

q: Two workflows use real-time calls: (1) a blocking pre-merge check developers wait on, and (2) an overnight technical-debt report. A manager wants both moved to the Message Batches API for 50% savings. Best evaluation?

choices.t: Move both workflows to the batch API and poll job status to know when each set of results completes.
Use batch for the overnight report only; keep synchronous calls for the blocking pre-merge check.
Keep both synchronous, since batch result-ordering issues would break correlating findings to files.
Move both to batch with a timeout that falls back to real-time calls if results aren't ready in time.

exp: Batch offers 50% savings but up to a 24-hour window with no latency SLA — fine for overnight jobs, unsuitable for blocking pre-merge checks. custom_id handles correlation, so ordering isn't a blocker; the fallback option adds needless complexity.

q: A 14-file PR reviewed in a single pass yields uneven depth, missed bugs, and contradictory feedback (flagging a pattern in one file while approving identical code elsewhere). How should you restructure the review?

choices.t: Run per-file analysis passes plus a separate cross-file integration pass, so depth is even and interactions surface.
Require developers to split large pull requests into three- or four-file chunks before submitting them.
Run three full-PR passes and report only the findings that appear in at least two of the independent runs.
Raise the context budget and keep the single pass, so all fourteen files fit without competing for attention.

exp: Attention thins across fourteen files in one pass, so the work splits: each file gets a full pass, and a separate pass looks only at what crosses between them. Asking developers to split the PR is the strongest alternative and would work, but it moves the constraint onto the humans rather than fixing the reviewer. Consensus across passes suppresses findings only one pass caught.

q: After each new commit your review bot re-posts comments it already made on earlier commits. How should the re-review avoid duplicates without losing coverage of the new code?

choices.t: Pass the prior findings into the review context and ask for only the new or still-unaddressed issues.
Review only the diff introduced since the last reviewed commit, so earlier code is not examined again.
Post each finding with a stable fingerprint and have the CI step skip any fingerprint posted before.
Delete the bot's previous comments before each run, so only the newest set of comments stays visible.

exp: Duplicates come from reviewing with no memory of what was already said, so the prior findings belong in context and the ask becomes what is new or unfixed. Reviewing only the new diff is the strongest alternative and is cheaper — but it misses issues in earlier commits that the new code has since made wrong. Fingerprints dedupe without knowing whether anything was addressed.

q: Your CI step asks Claude to generate tests for each pull request, and it produces broad tests for the whole file rather than the behavior the PR actually changed. What most improves the relevance?

choices.t: Scope the generation to the diff and supply the acceptance criteria for the change the pull request makes.
Supply the whole file alongside the diff, and ask for tests covering the changed behavior specifically.
Ask for fewer tests per pull request, so the model spends its budget on the most important behavior.
Run the generation after the merge, when the changed behavior has settled and the file stops moving.

exp: Relevance comes from telling the model what changed and what the change is meant to do, so the diff plus acceptance criteria is the input that matters. Supplying the whole file alongside is the strongest alternative and does give useful surrounding context — but it reintroduces the untouched behavior that pulled the output broad to begin with.

q: You need guaranteed schema-valid JSON with no syntax errors from extraction. Most reliable approach?

choices.t: Define a JSON schema, call the model with tool_use, and read the fields from the structured tool_use response.
Ask for JSON in the prompt, parse the text, and retry the call whenever parsing fails on a syntax error.
Prefill the assistant turn with an opening brace so the model continues into a well-formed JSON object.
Ask for JSON in the prompt and run a tolerant parser that repairs common syntax faults before reading it.

exp: tool_use with a schema makes the structure a property of the response rather than something recovered afterwards, which is what removes the syntax errors. Prompt-and-parse with retries is the strongest alternative and does converge eventually — it just pays for extra calls on a failure mode the schema prevents outright.

q: Some documents lack a tax_id field, and the model invents a value to satisfy the schema. What fixes this?

choices.t: Mark tax_id optional and nullable, so the model returns null when the document genuinely has no such value.
Keep tax_id required and add a separate has_tax_id boolean the consumer checks before reading the field.
Keep tax_id required and add a prompt instruction telling the model not to invent a value when it is absent.
Drop tax_id from the extraction schema, so the model is never asked for a field many documents simply lack.

exp: A required field with no honest empty value pushes the model to fabricate one, so optional and nullable gives the absence somewhere truthful to go. A has_tax_id flag is the strongest alternative and does record the absence — but the required field still has to be filled with something, so the fabrication survives alongside the flag.

q: Documents arrive in unknown types and you maintain several extraction schemas. You must guarantee the model calls one of the extraction tools rather than replying with chat text. Which setting fits?

choices.t: tool_choice set to "any", which requires a tool call while still letting the model pick the schema that fits.
tool_choice pinned to the extraction tool for the most common document type, with the others left available.
tool_choice set to "auto", with a prompt line instructing the model to always select an extraction tool.
tool_choice omitted, with the extraction tools listed first so the model reaches for them before replying.

exp: "any" makes a tool call mandatory without dictating which one, which is exactly what unknown document types need. Pinning the most common type is the strongest alternative and does guarantee a call — but it applies one schema to every document, so anything else is extracted against the wrong shape. "auto" permits a text reply whatever the prompt asks.

q: Your extractions are always valid JSON (via tool_use), but invoices sometimes have line items that don't sum to the stated total. What does tool_use NOT solve, and what helps?

choices.t: tool_use blocks syntax errors but not semantic ones; capture calculated_total beside stated_total and flag mismatches.
Add a schema constraint requiring the line-item total to equal the stated total, so tool_use rejects the mismatch.
Convert the numeric fields to strings so downstream code owns all of the arithmetic checking after extraction.
Return to prompt-only JSON output, where arithmetic mistakes are visible in the text before it is parsed.

exp: A schema enforces types and requiredness, not relationships between values, so a sum that does not reconcile is a semantic error the extraction layer cannot see. Capturing both totals turns it into a check you can run. The schema-constraint answer is the strongest alternative and describes the fix you would want — JSON Schema has no way to express it.

q: A required contract_end_date is missing from your extractions. On retry with the validation error appended, it still fails. Why is retry ineffective here?

choices.t: The date is not present in the source, and retry-with-feedback fixes format and structure rather than missing data.
The validation error is appended without the original document, so the model has nothing new to work from.
The schema marks contract_end_date required, and a required field cannot be corrected through a retry loop.
The retry reuses the earlier extraction, so the model repeats its previous answer instead of re-reading.

exp: Retry-with-feedback corrects how something was expressed; it cannot supply information the document does not contain. Re-supplying the document is the strongest alternative and is a genuine defect in many retry loops — but the premise is a retry that still carried the source, so the date is missing at the source itself.

q: Extraction quality drops on documents whose structure varies (inline citations vs bibliographies; tables vs narrative). Most effective technique?

choices.t: Add a few examples showing correct extraction across the varied document structures the pipeline sees.
Split the extraction into one schema per layout and classify the document before extracting from it.
Write longer prose instructions enumerating each document layout the extractor might encounter.
Reject documents that do not match the canonical layout, so only the expected structure is processed.

exp: Examples generalize across structural variety in a way prose does not: they show what an extraction looks like with an inline citation and with a bibliography. Classifying first and using per-layout schemas is the strongest alternative and is the right build once the layouts are stable and few — it adds a classification step that can itself be wrong on an unfamiliar document.

q: Overall extraction accuracy is 97%, so a teammate wants to drop human review entirely. What's the risk, and the right check?

choices.t: Aggregate accuracy hides weak types and fields, so stratify the measurement before cutting any review.
Cut review for the document types whose measured accuracy is highest and keep it for the remainder.
Keep review in place and add a second model that re-extracts every document, comparing the two results.
Treat 97% as sufficient and monitor downstream complaints as the signal that accuracy has slipped.

exp: A single aggregate can hide a document type at 70% behind a majority at 99%, so the number must be broken out by type and field before it can support the decision. Cutting review on the strongest types is the strongest alternative and is where this ends up — but it is the action, and the stratified measurement is what tells you which types qualify.

q: You have limited human reviewers and a calibrated field-level confidence score on every extraction. How should reviewer attention be targeted?

choices.t: Route the low-confidence and internally contradictory extractions to review, leaving the confident ones automated.
Route a fixed share of the lowest-confidence extractions each day, so reviewer load stays predictable.
Review a random ten percent of all extractions, so the sample stays representative of the population.
Route the longest documents to review, since more pages mean more opportunities for an extraction to go wrong.

exp: Scarce review should go where the risk is, and calibrated confidence plus internal contradictions is the signal that identifies it. Capping by volume is the strongest alternative and does make staffing predictable — but it fixes the number reviewed rather than the risk covered, so a bad day sends genuinely doubtful extractions straight through.

q: Your coordinator reliably covers broad topics but latency is high because it always fans out to 8+ subagents — even for narrow queries. When you cap subagents at 3, broad topics get incomplete coverage. Which design resolves both without a fixed cap?

choices.t: Keep the 8-subagent fan-out for every query but give each subagent a smaller token budget to cut latency.
Have the coordinator assess query breadth, dynamically pick subagent count and scope, then gap-check.
Always cap the fan-out at 3 subagents and instruct each one to cover more subtopics to keep coverage broad.
Alternate between 3 and 8 subagents on a fixed per-request schedule regardless of how broad the query is.

exp: Dynamic, breadth-driven decomposition plus an iterative coverage loop adapts to each query — unlike any fixed cap, token throttling, or fixed alternation.

q: You need two guarantees: identity verified before any refund, and refunds over $500 routed to a human. A teammate wants both in the system prompt “for simplicity.” For deterministic compliance, where should each live?

choices.t: Identity as a prerequisite gate blocking refund tools until get_customer verifies; the $500 limit as a system-prompt rule since amounts vary.
Both as few-shot examples in the prompt that demonstrate verifying identity first and escalating refunds above the $500 threshold.
Both as programmatic controls: a gate blocking refunds until get_customer verifies identity, and a hook blocking >$500 to escalation.
Identity verification as a system-prompt instruction; the $500 limit as a PostToolUse hook that logs any over-limit refund after it runs.

exp: Both are hard compliance rules with financial consequences, so both need programmatic enforcement. Prompt rules and examples are probabilistic; a PostToolUse log only records the violation after it happened.

q: To speed things up, the coordinator emits three Task calls in one turn to run subagents in parallel. The synthesis agent then produces shallow output missing those agents' findings — though parallelism itself is working. Most likely cause?

choices.t: Parallel Task calls can't be combined with a synthesis step, which requires strictly sequential spawning.
Synthesis was spawned without the parallel agents' results; their outputs must be passed explicitly.
The coordinator needs fork_session to merge the parallel branches back together before running synthesis.
The synthesis call's max_tokens is set too low to hold all of the parallel agents' findings at once.

exp: Parallel subagents have isolated context. Their results must be explicitly aggregated and injected into the synthesis prompt; nothing about parallelism forbids a downstream synthesis step.

q: Two tasks: (1) review a 30-file PR for the same five concern types in every file; (2) “harden this service against whatever failure modes you find.” Which decomposition fits each?

choices.t: Use prompt chaining for both tasks, prioritizing predictability even where the work is open-ended.
Use dynamic decomposition for both, on the reasoning that each task happens to touch multiple files.
(1) fixed per-file passes plus an integration pass; (2) dynamic decomposition driven by what you find.
(1) dynamic decomposition that re-plans per file; (2) a fixed prompt-chained pipeline for the hardening.

exp: Predictable multi-aspect reviews suit fixed prompt chaining; open-ended investigations suit adaptive decomposition that re-plans as it learns.

q: You finished a deep codebase analysis and now want to compare two refactoring strategies that both start from that exact analysis, without re-running it. Best mechanism?

choices.t: Run --resume on the same named session twice and hope the two strategies' state doesn't collide or overwrite.
Use fork_session to branch two independent sessions from the shared analysis baseline without re-running it.
Start two fresh sessions and paste the entire codebase into each again so both begin from the same analysis.
Run /compact to shrink the analysis, then ask for both refactoring strategies within one single session.

exp: fork_session branches divergent explorations from a shared baseline. Resuming one session twice collides; fresh restarts discard the analysis; one compacted session can't keep the two explorations independent.

q: An engineer ends the agent loop when the model's text says “Let me know if you need anything else.” Intermittently the loop halts while a tool call was still pending. Best correction?

choices.t: Keep matching assistant prose but add more completion phrases to the text matcher so it catches every variant the model produces.
Terminate on stop_reason == end_turn and continue on tool_use; never parse assistant prose as a completion signal.
Add a 15-iteration cap as the primary stop condition so the loop always halts after fifteen turns regardless of stop_reason.
Stop the loop as soon as the model returns any text content, treating the first piece of assistant text as completion.

exp: Loop control must follow stop_reason. Matching prose, using an arbitrary cap as the primary stop, or treating any text as completion are the named anti-patterns.

q: To cut latency, a developer lets subagents call each other directly (search → analysis → synthesis), bypassing the coordinator. Now error handling is inconsistent and failures are hard to see. Which hub-and-spoke property was sacrificed?

choices.t: Nothing meaningful was lost — letting subagents call each other directly is strictly faster and better.
Centralized routing through the coordinator, which gives observability and consistent error handling.
Hub-and-spoke only affects how much parallelism is possible, not error handling or failure visibility.
The fix is to give every subagent the Task tool so each one can spawn its own peers when it needs to.

exp: Routing all inter-subagent communication through the coordinator is what gives observability and consistent error handling; bypassing it trades those away.

q: A single agent reviewing 25 files at once gives deep feedback on the first and last few files and superficial notes in the middle. Beyond splitting passes, which effect explains the middle gap, and what ordering helps when you must aggregate?

choices.t: Token starvation is the cause; raise max_tokens and keep reviewing all files in one single pass.
It is the lost-in-the-middle effect; put key summaries up front and use explicit section headers.
Temperature variance is the cause; set temperature to 0 so the middle files get equal attention.
Model laziness is the cause; instruct it to try harder on every file so the middle isn't skipped.

exp: Models process the beginning and end of long inputs more reliably than the middle. Position-aware ordering — summaries up front, explicit headers — mitigates it.

q: The agent escalates mid-resolution to a human who cannot see the conversation transcript. What must the handoff include to be useful?

choices.t: A short note saying the customer needs help, plus a link to the chat UI so the human can open and read the conversation themselves.
The full raw conversation transcript pasted verbatim, with no summary, so the human has every detail of the exchange available.
A structured summary: customer ID, root-cause analysis, refund amount, and the recommended action for the human to take.
Only the customer's computed sentiment score and a priority flag, so the human knows how urgent and frustrated the case is.

exp: Since the human lacks the transcript, the handoff must be a structured summary with the key facts and a recommended action.

q: Your coordinator prompt gives subagents rigid step-by-step procedures, and they fail to adapt when sources turn out sparse. Better prompt design?

choices.t: Add even more detailed procedural steps to the coordinator prompt to cover every possible contingency.
Specify research goals and quality criteria, not step-by-step procedures, so subagents can adapt.
Remove all guidance from the coordinator prompt and let each subagent do whatever it decides to do.
Force a specific tool first with tool_choice on every subagent so their first action is always fixed.

exp: Goal- and criteria-oriented coordinator prompts enable subagent adaptability; brittle procedures and zero guidance both fail, and forcing a tool addresses a different concern.

q: Despite well-written descriptions, the agent still misroutes “analyze this invoice” to analyze_content instead of extract_invoice. The system prompt says “always analyze customer content carefully.” Most likely culprit and fix?

choices.t: The tool descriptions are still too short to disambiguate; add worked examples inside each description so routing improves.
The model is sampling too randomly between the tools; lower the temperature so routing becomes deterministic and consistent.
Keyword-sensitive prompt wording (analyze content) creates an association that overrides the descriptions; revise the wording.
Having two similar tools is the root problem; merge analyze_content and extract_invoice into one tool to remove the choice entirely.

exp: Keyword-sensitive system-prompt instructions can override even good tool descriptions. Reviewing and revising that wording is the fix.

q: A search subagent hits a transient timeout on one of five queries; the other four succeed. Best error strategy?

choices.t: Immediately propagate the timeout to the coordinator and discard the four successful query results.
Retry the transient query locally; propagate only if unresolved, with partial results and context.
Mark the whole search as failed so the coordinator restarts it, including the four queries that succeeded.
Return the four successful queries as a complete result and silently drop the one that timed out.

exp: Subagents should recover locally from transient failures and propagate only unresolved errors, with partial results — never silently drop or over-propagate.

q: Enrichment tools must never run before metadata extraction. Within a single model turn, how do you guarantee extract_metadata is called first?

choices.t: Set tool_choice to "any" and hope the model happens to pick extract_metadata before any enrichment tool.
Force it with tool_choice {type:tool, name:extract_metadata}, then handle enrichment in follow-up turns.
Put "call extract_metadata first" in the system prompt only, which is guidance and not a hard guarantee.
Give the agent only the enrichment tools and no extraction tool, which blocks the required step entirely.

exp: Forced tool selection guarantees the first call; subsequent steps proceed in follow-up turns. “any” and prompt instructions are not guarantees.

q: You need standard Jira integration plus a bespoke internal deployment-tracking workflow. Build vs adopt?

choices.t: Build both servers custom for consistency, reinventing a standard Jira integration that already exists.
Adopt a community MCP server for Jira; build a custom server only for the team-specific deployment flow.
Use community servers for both and force-fit the bespoke deployment workflow into a generic integration.
Avoid MCP entirely and script both the Jira and deployment workflows with ad-hoc Bash commands instead.

exp: Adopt community servers for standard integrations; build custom only for genuinely team-specific workflows.

q: A refund violates a policy cap, and the agent keeps retrying it, burning calls. What error design stops the retries while still communicating well to the customer?

choices.t: Return a generic Operation failed message with no detail, so the agent treats it as terminal and gives up on the refund.
Return the error with isRetryable:true so the agent can automatically retry with a smaller amount that fits the policy cap.
Return the business error with retriable:false plus a customer-friendly explanation, so the agent stops retrying.
Throw an unhandled exception on the policy violation that aborts the conversation entirely rather than returning an error result.

exp: Business/validation errors should carry retriable:false and a human-readable reason. Generic failures lose context, and a retryable flag invites pointless retries.

q: An agent with a generic fetch_url tool sometimes pulls arbitrary, irrelevant pages. You want it to load only validated documents. Best change?

choices.t: Keep the generic fetch_url tool but add "only fetch documents" to the prompt, which is weak guidance.
Replace fetch_url with a constrained load_document tool that validates document URLs by contract.
Add more tools so the agent has additional options, increasing selection load without constraining it.
Set tool_choice to "any" to force a tool call, which still permits the agent to fetch arbitrary pages.

exp: Replacing a generic tool with a constrained, purpose-specific one (with a defined contract) is more reliable than prompt guidance.

q: Why does conflating “search returned zero matches” with “search failed” specifically harm a research coordinator's decisions?

choices.t: It only affects how verbose the coordinator's logs are; the actual recovery decisions stay unaffected.
The two warrant opposite actions, so conflating them drives the coordinator to wrong recovery choices.
It causes JSON schema violations downstream that corrupt the structured data the coordinator receives.
It roughly doubles token usage for the coordinator, but the recovery decisions themselves are unaffected.

exp: Empty-but-successful and access-failure require opposite responses, so the coordinator must be able to tell them apart.

q: Conventions for **/*.test.tsx must apply to test files scattered across many directories and load automatically only when editing those files. Which mechanism — and why not the alternatives?

choices.t: Place a subdirectory CLAUDE.md in each folder that contains tests so the conventions load when editing them.
Use .claude/rules/ files with YAML frontmatter glob paths, which load automatically by file pattern across dirs.
Put the test conventions in a skill under .claude/skills/, which applies automatically whenever a test file is being edited.
Keep one monolithic root CLAUDE.md with a “tests” section that covers every test file across all directories.

exp: Path-glob rules load conditionally by file pattern across directories. Subdir CLAUDE.md can't follow files spread everywhere, skills aren't automatic, and a monolith always loads regardless of file.

q: A codebase-analysis skill floods the main conversation with verbose output, derailing later steps. Which frontmatter option fixes this, and what does it do?

choices.t: allowed-tools, which restricts which tools the skill may call but does not isolate its verbose output.
context: fork, which runs the skill in an isolated subagent so its verbose output stays out of the chat.
argument-hint, which prompts the user for a missing argument and has nothing to do with output volume.
model: haiku, which runs the skill on a smaller model but still pollutes the main session with its output.

exp: context: fork isolates verbose or exploratory skills in a subagent context, keeping the main conversation clean. The other options serve different purposes.

q: Each package needs only its relevant standards, and a monolithic CLAUDE.md has grown unwieldy. Cleanest way to keep each package's CLAUDE.md focused?

choices.t: Duplicate the full standards into every package's CLAUDE.md so each package carries exactly what it needs.
Use @import in each package's CLAUDE.md to selectively pull in only the standards files relevant to it.
Move all the shared standards up into the user-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md so every package inherits them.
Delete the shared standards entirely and rely only on per-file rules to convey each package's conventions.

exp: @import keeps CLAUDE.md modular by referencing external standards files per package. Duplication and user-level placement don't scale or share correctly.

q: Your CI uses the same Claude session to generate code and then review it, and subtle bugs slip through. Beyond prompting, what structural change helps most?

choices.t: Add a 'review critically' instruction to the same session so it scrutinizes the code it just wrote.
Run the review in an independent Claude instance without the generator's reasoning context.
Increase the generating session's max_tokens so it has room to reason more thoroughly during review.
Re-run generation twice in the session and diff the two outputs to surface the subtle bugs slipping by.

exp: An independent review instance (no generation context) catches subtle issues that self-review in the same session misses.

q: A library migration affects 45+ files with two viable approaches that differ in infrastructure. Most effective workflow?

choices.t: Use direct execution throughout, switching to plan mode only later if serious problems happen to emerge.
Use plan mode to explore and choose the approach, then switch to direct execution to implement the chosen plan.
Stay in plan mode for the entire migration, planning and then re-planning every individual edit across all 45 files.
Use direct execution driven by one massive upfront instruction that covers all 45 files in a single pass.

exp: Plan for the investigation and architectural decision, then execute directly. Pure direct execution risks rework; staying in plan mode for every edit is unnecessary.

q: You have (a) universal standards that should always apply and (b) a verbose, occasional “generate migration script” workflow. Where does each belong?

choices.t: Put both the universal standards and the migration workflow in CLAUDE.md so they're always loaded.
(a) CLAUDE.md, always loaded; (b) an on-demand skill, with context: fork for its verbose output.
Make both into skills to keep CLAUDE.md small, even though the universal standards should always apply.
(a) as an on-demand skill; (b) in CLAUDE.md, inverting where always-on versus occasional logic belongs.

exp: Always-on universal standards belong in CLAUDE.md; task-specific on-demand workflows belong in skills, forked when their output is verbose.

q: Claude behaves inconsistently across sessions — sometimes following a convention, sometimes not. Which command helps diagnose which memory files are actually loaded?

choices.t: Run /compact to shrink the context, which reveals which memory files are loaded across the sessions.
Run /memory to see exactly which memory files are currently loaded into the session.
Run /resume to reload the last session and surface which memory files it pulls back into context.
Run /clear to wipe the context and retry, exposing which memory files reload on the fresh start.

exp: /memory shows which memory files are loaded, the right tool for diagnosing inconsistent cross-session behavior.

q: You want to batch-extract 5,000 invoices overnight using a multi-tool agent that calls tools mid-request to validate as it goes. Why might the Message Batches API be the wrong fit?

choices.t: The batch API can't accept 5,000 documents in a single submission window, so the overnight job won't fit.
The batch API can't run multi-turn tool calling in one request, so it can't execute tools mid-request.
The batch API provides no cost savings on extraction workloads, so it defeats the point of going overnight.
The batch API guarantees sub-second latency you don't need, making it the wrong tool for an overnight run.

exp: Batch requests can't do in-request multi-turn tool calling. If your extraction depends on calling tools mid-request, batch won't work as designed.

q: Batch processing can take up to 24 hours. You must guarantee findings are ready within 30 hours of a document arriving. What submission cadence works?

choices.t: Submit one batch daily at midnight regardless of when each document actually arrived during the day.
Wait until 5,000 documents accumulate, then submit them together as a single large overnight batch.
Submit batches every ~4-6 hours so worst-case 24h processing plus the wait still meets the 30h SLA.
Use synchronous calls instead, since the batch API can never reliably meet any time-bound SLA at all.

exp: Bound the pre-submission wait so wait + 24h ≤ 30h. Frequent fixed windows guarantee the SLA; daily or volume-triggered submission can blow past it.

q: Two failures: (i) the model put the vendor name in the buyer field; (ii) a required clause date isn't anywhere in the document. Which is fixable by retry-with-error-feedback?

choices.t: Both are fixable, because retrying the call with the validation error appended always helps the model recover.
Only (i), a structural placement error; (ii) is data missing from the source and won't be fixed by retrying.
Neither is fixable, because tool_use outputs are final and can't be retried with error feedback at all.
Only (ii), because supplying information that is missing from the source is exactly what retries are for.

exp: Retries correct format/placement errors but cannot supply information that isn't in the source.

q: Your reviewer's “comment-accuracy” checks have a ~40% false-positive rate, eroding trust in its otherwise accurate security findings. Pragmatic move while you fix the prompt?

choices.t: Keep the noisy category enabled but tell developers to just ignore its frequent false positives.
Temporarily disable the high-false-positive category to restore trust, then fix it offline.
Disable the accurate security category instead, cutting total comment volume to make the bot quieter.
Lower the model temperature globally so the reviewer stops producing so many false-positive comments.

exp: High-false-positive categories undermine confidence in the accurate ones. Disable the noisy category temporarily and fix its criteria.

q: A document_type field must classify known types but also handle novel ones without fabrication or rigid failure. Best schema design?

choices.t: Use an enum of known types plus an "other" value with a free-text detail field, and "unclear" for ambiguity.
Use a required free-text string with no enum at all so the model writes whatever type label it infers each time.
Use a strict enum with no escape value, hard-rejecting any document whose type isn't already in the fixed list.
Use a separate boolean per known type, leaving every novel document with all of its flags set to false and unlabeled.

exp: Enum + “other”+detail (and “unclear”) gives extensible categorization without forcing fabrication or hard failure.

q: Your reviewer flags an idiomatic pattern as a bug in some files but not others. You want consistent judgment that generalizes to new variants — not a hardcoded allowlist. Best technique?

choices.t: Maintain a regex allowlist of acceptable code snippets so the reviewer never flags those exact patterns.
Add a prompt line telling the model not to flag idiomatic code so it stops treating the pattern as a bug.
Add few-shot examples contrasting the acceptable pattern with genuine issues so the model generalizes.
Disable the entire category so the idiomatic pattern can no longer be flagged inconsistently as a bug.

exp: Few-shot examples that show the reasoning generalize beyond pre-specified cases, unlike brittle allowlists or vague instructions.

q: Source documents sometimes contain internally inconsistent figures. How can the extraction itself surface this for downstream handling?

choices.t: Force the model to choose the figure it judges more likely correct and emit only that single resolved value each time.
Add calculated_total, stated_total, and a conflict_detected boolean so discrepancies are flagged downstream.
Drop any document that contains internally inconsistent figures so that only clean documents ever reach extraction.
Average the inconsistent figures into one combined value and store that as the document's single final total.

exp: Self-checking fields (calculated vs stated, conflict_detected) surface semantic conflicts for downstream decisions instead of hiding them.

q: Order lookups return 40+ fields but only ~5 matter for returns. Over a long chat, context fills with noise and recall degrades. Best fix?

choices.t: Increase max_tokens for each request so all 40 returned fields fit in context without the model losing track of any of them.
Trim tool outputs to only the return-relevant fields before they accumulate in the conversation context.
Summarize the entire conversation on every turn so accumulated order data is condensed and the context stays small.
Move the full 40-field order payloads into CLAUDE.md so they live outside the chat but stay available to the model.

exp: Trimming verbose tool outputs to the relevant fields controls context growth; larger budgets and aggressive summarization don't address the noise at its source.

q: A field-level report shows 99% overall accuracy, but you suspect a hidden weak spot. Which analysis most reliably reveals it before automating?

choices.t: Trust the 99% aggregate and spot-check ten randomly chosen documents before automating away the human review step.
Stratify accuracy by type and field and sample high-confidence extractions to catch novel errors.
Increase the number of required fields in the schema to push the aggregate accuracy figure even higher than before.
Re-run extraction with a second model and compare the totals, treating any agreement as proof of correctness here.

exp: Aggregates mask weak segments. Stratifying by type/field and sampling high-confidence outputs exposes hidden failure modes before you reduce review.

q: A long multi-agent codebase exploration crashes midway. What design lets the coordinator resume without redoing everything?

choices.t: Rely on --resume to automatically restore all in-memory agent state so the run continues from where it crashed.
Have each agent export structured state to a known location and load a manifest on resume to re-inject it.
Re-run the entire multi-agent exploration from scratch, since crash recovery means starting the whole job over.
Keep all exploration state only in the main conversation context so the coordinator can read it back on resume.

exp: Structured state exports plus a manifest the coordinator loads on resume enable crash recovery without full re-exploration.
