q: A synthesis report mixes financial figures, news, and technical findings. To preserve meaning, how should it render them?

choices.t: Convert every section to bullet points so the financial, news, and technical content all look consistent.
Render each appropriately — finances as tables, news as prose, technical findings as lists.
Convert every section to flowing prose paragraphs so the whole report reads in one uniform style.
Convert the financial, news, and technical content into one large JSON blob for the reader to parse.

exp: Content-type-appropriate rendering preserves meaning; uniform flattening loses the structure that makes each type readable.

q: Which situation is a legitimate escalation trigger that agents most often miss?

choices.t: The customer used a frustrated, angry tone even though the underlying request itself is routine and the policy clearly covers it.
The model's self-reported confidence dipped just below 7 out of 10 on a case that is otherwise easy and well within policy.
The policy is silent or ambiguous on the request, such as competitor price-matching when it only covers own-site adjustments.
The case involves many sequential steps to complete, even though a clear and directly applicable policy governs every one of them.

exp: Policy gaps/ambiguity are valid escalation triggers. Sentiment, self-reported confidence, and mere step count are unreliable proxies for complexity.

q: A downstream synthesis agent has a tight context budget and is receiving verbose reasoning chains from upstream agents. What should upstream agents return instead?

choices.t: Return even longer, more verbose outputs to the synthesis agent so that no upstream detail is ever missed.
Return structured data — key facts, citations, and relevance scores — instead of reasoning chains.
Return only a single one-word summary per source so the tight downstream context budget is never exceeded.
Return raw tool dumps and let the budget-constrained synthesis agent parse and condense them itself.

exp: When downstream budgets are tight, upstream agents should emit compact structured data (facts, citations, scores), not verbose reasoning.

q: Your support agent answers the first turn fine, but on the second turn it has forgotten the customer ID from get_customer and re-verifies the customer. The backend forwards only the newest user message to the API. What is the root cause?

choices.t: The Claude API is stateless, so every call must resend the conversation, including the prior tool_use and tool_result blocks.
The conversation exceeded the context window after the first turn, so the earliest blocks were dropped before the second call.
The backend is omitting the session identifier the API needs in order to associate the second turn with the first.
Tool results live only in the execution layer and must be written to a store the model reads back at the start of each turn.

exp: Claude's API keeps no server-side memory, so a backend forwarding only the newest user message erases the earlier tool_use and tool_result blocks. A context-window overflow is the most plausible alternative, but two turns of a support conversation come nowhere near the limit, and an overflow would degrade gradually rather than lose exactly the prior turn.

q: Mid-resolution the agent's response returns with stop_reason "max_tokens" while it was still listing a customer's eligible refunds. Your loop treats any non-tool_use stop_reason as completion. What is the correct handling?

choices.t: Treat max_tokens as truncation rather than completion, and either raise the limit or continue the generation so the turn finishes.
Treat max_tokens like end_turn and finalize, since the model stopped emitting output and the turn has therefore ended.
Treat max_tokens as a transient failure and resend the identical request, expecting the next attempt to run to completion.
Treat max_tokens as a signal to escalate, since a turn that could not finish is one the agent cannot recover from alone.

exp: max_tokens means the response was cut off mid-generation: the content is incomplete, not final. Raising the limit or continuing the generation finishes the turn. Only end_turn signals completion, resending unchanged reproduces the same truncation, and escalating hands a human a problem the loop can fix itself.

q: A customer asks about order #501 and order #777 in one message, both on the same account. Your agent calls get_customer once per order, re-fetching the identical profile and doubling latency. What is the better pattern?

choices.t: Verify the customer once, then investigate both orders in parallel against that shared profile before synthesizing one reply.
Verify once and cache the profile for the conversation, then work the two orders in sequence so each result informs the next.
Issue one lookup_order call covering #501 and #777 together, so a single request returns everything the reply needs.
Keep the per-order fetch but trim each profile response, so the duplicated call costs less on the second investigation.

exp: The two orders are independent, so one verification plus parallel investigation removes both the duplicate fetch and the serial wait. Caching and then working sequentially is the strongest alternative and does fix the duplicate call, which was the stated symptom — but it leaves the second order waiting on the first for no reason. Collapsing distinct orders into one lookup conflates them.

q: A teammate wants a fixed if/else decision tree (“if the message mentions refund, call process_refund; else call lookup_order”) instead of letting the model select tools. What is the strongest argument for the model-driven agentic loop here?

choices.t: It selects each next action from context and prior results, handling issue combinations no fixed tree was written to anticipate.
It removes the maintenance burden of a routing table that must be edited whenever a tool or a customer phrasing is added.
It lets new tools be added without a redeploy, since the model discovers each new capability from its description alone.
It produces cheaper turns, because the model skips the tools a decision tree would have called on the way to an answer.

exp: The loop's advantage is adaptivity: Claude picks the next action from what the previous tool actually returned, which is what a static tree cannot do for a message bundling three issues. Lower maintenance is the strongest alternative and is genuinely true — but it is a consequence of the adaptivity rather than the reason to choose it. Cost is not systematically lower either way.

q: lookup_order returns dates as Unix timestamps, while a separate shipping MCP tool returns them as "Mar 5, 2025". The agent keeps misreading and comparing them inconsistently. What is the cleanest way to normalize before the model sees them?

choices.t: Add a PostToolUse hook that rewrites each tool's dates into one canonical format before the result is appended to context.
Ask the MCP server owners to emit ISO 8601 at the source, so every tool in the fleet returns the same date shape.
Add a system-prompt instruction telling the model to convert every date it reads into ISO 8601 before comparing them.
Add a few-shot example comparing a Unix timestamp with a text date, so the model learns the conversion it needs.

exp: Normalizing in a hook is deterministic and applies to every result before the model sees it. Fixing the format upstream is the cleanest answer when you own the servers — here one is a third party, so it is slow at best and outside your control at worst. Prompt instructions and examples leave the conversion to the model.

q: You have two rules: (a) refunds must never exceed a per-customer eligibility cap, and (b) the agent should prefer a warm, apologetic tone when declining. A teammate wants both enforced as PreToolUse hooks. Where should each rule live?

choices.t: Both as PreToolUse hooks, since enforcing them in code guarantees the cap and the apologetic tone on every single response.
The eligibility cap as a PreToolUse hook; the tone as a system-prompt preference, since tone is soft guidance, not a hard rule.
Both as system-prompt instructions, since a single well-written prompt can reliably guarantee the cap and the tone together here.
The tone as a PreToolUse hook and the cap as a system-prompt rule, enforcing style in code while leaving the money rule to prose.

exp: Hooks give deterministic guarantees and fit hard rules with financial consequences like the cap; tone is a soft preference well suited to the prompt. Putting tone in a hook is impractical, and leaving the money cap to prose makes a critical rule merely probabilistic.

q: You are filling in the support agent's AgentDefinition. The workflow needs get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, and escalate_to_human. A colleague suggests also adding Task "just in case" it ever wants helper subagents. Best allowed_tools choice?

choices.t: List only the four tools the role uses, adding Task later if a real delegation need actually appears.
Add Task alongside the four now, so the agent is ready to delegate the moment a workflow needs a subagent.
List every backend tool the company exposes, so this one agent can resolve any request without a config change.
Leave allowed_tools empty and let the system prompt describe which tools the agent may call on each turn.

exp: Least privilege scopes allowed_tools to what the role actually uses; Task is added when delegation is real rather than speculative. Adding it now widens the selection space for a capability nothing calls, listing the full catalog does so dramatically, and an empty allowed_tools grants no tool access at all.

q: A customer opens with "This is outrageous, your product is garbage!" but has not asked for a human. The underlying issue is a damaged item your agent can refund. What is the best first move?

choices.t: Escalate to a human immediately, treating the strongly negative tone as an implicit request to speak with a manager about this.
Acknowledge the frustration, offer a concrete resolution (replacement or refund), and escalate only if the customer insists.
Run a sentiment score on the message and escalate automatically if the measured frustration crosses a preset anger threshold.
Ignore the emotional wording and proceed straight to processing the refund without acknowledging the customer's complaint.

exp: Acknowledge emotion, then propose a resolution, and escalate only if the customer reiterates wanting a human. Frustration alone isn't a request for a manager, sentiment scores don't track case complexity, and skipping acknowledgment ignores a valid concern.

q: After resolving order #501's refund your agent ends the turn, but the customer's original message also mentioned a wrong shipping address it never touched. Customers keep reopening tickets for the dropped second issue. Which design most reliably prevents this?

choices.t: Track every decomposed issue and require each to be resolved or explicitly deferred before the conversation is allowed to close.
Have the agent restate all the issues it identified at the start of its reply, so an unaddressed one is visible to the customer.
Add a closing checklist to the system prompt instructing the agent to confirm each raised issue before ending the turn.
Add a review pass that reads each closed transcript and reopens any ticket where a raised issue was never answered.

exp: The dropped issue is a state problem: nothing tracked that two items were opened and only one closed, so closure has to be conditional on every item being resolved or deferred. Restating the issues up front is the strongest alternative and genuinely helps, but it relies on the customer noticing the omission. The prompt checklist is the same probabilistic guarantee that already failed.

q: Policy requires the customer to see a refund preview (amount, fees, ETA) and confirm before money moves. Your process_refund tool has a preview_only flag, but the agent often skips straight to preview_only=false. What most reliably enforces preview-then-confirm?

choices.t: Split it into preview_refund, returning a single-use confirmation token, and execute_refund, which requires that token.
Add detailed instructions and few-shot examples to the tool description telling the agent to always preview before executing.
Keep one tool but have the server allow preview_only=false only if a matching preview ran for that customer in the last minute.
Lower the temperature so the agent stops skipping the preview step and reliably calls preview_only=true before charging.

exp: Two tools bound by a single-use token make execution architecturally impossible without a prior preview. Instructions and examples rely on model compliance, a time-window heuristic is brittle and can mismatch params, and temperature doesn't enforce ordering.

q: get_customer accepts either an email or a numeric customer_id, but its description says only “Finds a customer.” The agent often passes an order number or a full name and the call fails. Which change most directly reduces the malformed calls?

choices.t: Expand the description to state the accepted formats with examples — an email like user@x.com, or a numeric id — and what it returns.
Split it into get_customer_by_email and get_customer_by_id, so each tool's single input type is unambiguous at selection time.
Accept a single generic string and resolve the format server-side, returning a validation error when it matches neither shape.
Wrap the tool so it tries the value as an email, then as an id, then as a name, returning the first record that matches.

exp: The description is the model's only guide to a tool's inputs, so stating the accepted formats with examples fixes malformed arguments at the source. Splitting into two typed tools is the strongest alternative and removes the ambiguity outright — but it adds a tool and a selection decision to solve what one description edit solves. Name-matching can silently return the wrong customer.

q: lookup_order fails about 10% of the time: most are brief network timeouts that succeed on a second attempt, the rest are malformed-order-id errors that never will. Both return the same error today. Which tool-side design best stops the wasted retries?

choices.t: Retry the transient timeouts inside the tool with backoff, and return malformed-id errors immediately with validation detail.
Return both unchanged but tag each with a retryable flag, letting the agent decide whether a second attempt is worthwhile.
Apply one exponential-backoff policy to every failure, so the tool's recovery behavior stays uniform and easy to reason about.
Classify every failure as a malformed id and return it as terminal, prompting the agent to ask the customer to re-enter it.

exp: The tool is the only layer that knows which failure it hit, so it absorbs the transient ones itself and fails fast on the ones that never succeed. Tagging both with a retryable flag is the strongest alternative and is the right shape when the caller has context the tool lacks — here it spends an agent turn on recovery the tool could have done silently. Uniform backoff waits on errors that never clear.

q: Before answering refund-eligibility questions the agent burns three or four tool calls discovering which policies and order statuses exist. Which MCP capability removes that discovery overhead without enlarging the tool catalog?

choices.t: Expose the refund policy and the order-status catalog as MCP resources the agent reads as context, with no action call.
Add one read-only get_policy tool that returns the whole catalog, so a single call replaces the exploratory sequence.
Add a dedicated fetch tool per policy document, giving the agent a precise tool for each kind of eligibility question.
Include the full policy and status reference in the system prompt so it is loaded before the first turn of every ticket.

exp: Resources are read-only context the agent consults without spending an action call or a slot in the tool catalog, which is exactly the overhead described. A single get_policy tool is the strongest alternative and does collapse the sequence to one call — but it still costs a turn and a tool definition for data that never changes mid-conversation. A tool per document multiplies selection load.

q: A long resolution involves verify, lookup, refund, and notify steps. Mid-flow the worker process crashes and restarts; on restart it re-verifies and re-refunds, risking a double refund. What design lets it resume safely without repeating completed steps?

choices.t: Rely on session resume to automatically restore the in-memory step state so the worker continues exactly where it crashed.
Re-run the entire flow from the first step on every restart, accepting that crash recovery means redoing all of the prior work.
Persist structured step state to a known location and, on restart, load it to resume from the last completed step.
Keep all step state only in the conversation context, trusting the model to recall which steps it already finished before.

exp: Exporting structured step state and reloading it on restart lets the worker skip completed steps and avoid the double refund. In-memory state is lost on a crash, re-running everything repeats side effects, and conversation context alone isn't a durable record of progress.

q: In a long ticket, the prompt grows to many turns with the verified customer ID and refund amount buried in the middle. The agent reliably uses facts near the start and end but misreads the buried ones. What ordering best mitigates this?

choices.t: Put the case facts — customer ID, refund amount — at the top of the prompt and the requested action at the end, off the middle.
Re-state the case facts in the final user turn as well, so they sit in the recency window the model attends to most closely.
Move the case facts into the exact middle of the prompt and mark them with bold delimiters so they stand out from the history.
Summarize the middle of the conversation every turn so the buried facts are rewritten closer to the current position.

exp: Recall is strongest at the beginning and end of a long input, so key facts belong at the top and the action at the end. Re-stating them in the last turn is the strongest alternative and works for the same reason — it is a narrower version of the same fix, leaving one copy in the recency window. Bold markers do not move the weak region, and per-turn summarization is what blurred the figures.

q: The agent has tried two reasonable approaches to a stuck order and neither worked. The customer has not asked for a human, policy clearly covers the case, and no remaining tool is likely to help. What is the appropriate next step?

choices.t: Escalate with a structured handoff recording both attempts and their outcomes, since progress has stopped despite reasonable effort.
Tell the customer what was tried and that it failed, then offer to escalate, letting them choose whether to wait for a human.
Try a third variation of the same two approaches, since policy covers the case and a further attempt may still resolve it.
Hold off on escalating, since the customer never requested a human and the policy leaves no ambiguity to hand off.

exp: Being unable to make progress is itself an escalation trigger, independent of whether the customer asked; the handoff carries what was already tried so the human does not repeat it. Offering the choice is the strongest alternative and is better when the agent still has an untried option — here there is none, so it asks the customer to decide what the agent already knows.

q: You must extract a shared auth helper from an unfamiliar service, and two plausible module boundaries are already visible. You have not read the code yet. Which workflow fits best?

choices.t: Use plan mode to read the code and settle the boundary, then switch to direct execution to apply the approved plan.
Read the two candidate modules directly first, then start executing once the boundary is obvious from the code itself.
Stay in plan mode for the whole task, re-planning before each edit so nothing changes without an approval step.
Skip planning and write one instruction specifying both candidate boundaries, letting the model choose as it works.

exp: Unfamiliar code plus a genuine design fork is what plan mode is for: explore safely, settle the boundary, then execute the approved plan. Reading the modules first is the strongest alternative and reaches the same understanding — but it leaves the decision undocumented and unapproved, which is the part that matters when two boundaries are both viable.

q: Your /scaffold-module skill needs a target directory to work, but teammates keep invoking it bare and it guesses wrong. Which SKILL.md frontmatter field addresses this directly?

choices.t: Add argument-hint describing the expected directory, so invoking the skill bare prompts the developer for that argument.
Set allowed-tools to the file tools the skill needs, so its actions stay within the directory it is meant to touch.
Set context: fork so the skill runs in an isolated subagent and its directory scan stays out of the main session.
Move the skill into .claude/rules/ with a paths glob so it activates only while files in that directory are open.

exp: argument-hint documents the parameter a skill expects and surfaces a prompt for it when the skill is invoked bare, which is exactly the failure described. allowed-tools constrains which tools may run, context: fork isolates output, and a rules glob governs when something loads — none of them ask the developer for a missing argument.

q: A shared /generate-tests skill should write new test files but has twice deleted source files by mistake. You want a hard guarantee it can never delete, without rewriting its prompt. Best approach?

choices.t: Add a strongly worded line to the skill body forbidding deletion, so the model treats removing any source file as off-limits.
Set context: fork on the skill so it runs in a subagent, isolating its actions from the main session and its files.
Set allowed-tools on the skill to the read/write/edit tools it needs and omit Bash, so deletion isn't in its capability set.
Move the skill to ~/.claude/skills/ so it is personal, which narrows who runs it but leaves its tool capabilities unchanged.

exp: allowed-tools restricts which tools a skill may use, so omitting the tool that can delete makes deletion impossible — an enforcement guarantee, not guidance. A prompt prohibition is probabilistic, context: fork isolates output not capabilities, and changing scope to user-level doesn't remove the delete tool.

q: Only the packages/legacy-api folder still follows older naming and error-handling conventions; the rest of the repo uses the modern style. You want those conventions to apply just there, shared with the team. Where do they belong?

choices.t: Put a CLAUDE.md inside packages/legacy-api, so the conventions apply when working in that folder and ship with the repo.
Append a legacy-api section to the root CLAUDE.md, where it sits alongside the modern conventions for the whole repo.
Add the legacy conventions to each developer's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, where per-developer working preferences are kept.
Record the conventions in a /memory note taken while working in that folder, so they are recalled in later sessions.

exp: A CLAUDE.md inside the folder scopes its conventions to that part of the tree and travels with the repository. A root-level section would apply the legacy naming to the modern code as well, the user-level file is personal and unversioned, and /memory writes into a CLAUDE.md rather than scoping rules to a directory.

q: Database migration files live in many folders, and their conventions matter only while one is being edited. Today they sit in the root CLAUDE.md and load on every request. What is the best fix?

choices.t: Move them into a .claude/rules/ file with a paths glob for the migration files, so they load only when one is edited.
Put a CLAUDE.md in each migrations folder, so the conventions load exactly when work happens inside one of them.
Keep them in the root CLAUDE.md under a heading noting they apply only to migrations, so the model can scope them itself.
Keep them in the root CLAUDE.md and rely on /compact to trim the migration rules back out once context grows large.

exp: A rules file with a paths glob matches by file pattern across every folder, so one definition covers all the migration directories and costs nothing until a matching file is opened. A CLAUDE.md per folder is the strongest alternative and loads just as conditionally — but it duplicates the same rules across many directories, where they drift apart.

q: You hand Claude a one-line request — “add caching to the report endpoint” — and the result keeps missing concerns you never mentioned, like invalidation and stale reads. What most effectively surfaces those before it writes code?

choices.t: Have Claude interview you with clarifying questions first, so the non-obvious concerns surface before any code is written.
Write the request as a specification enumerating the caching concerns the endpoint needs, and hand that over instead.
Let it implement its best guess, then review the result and file the gaps as follow-up work once they are visible.
Ask it to list its assumptions alongside the implementation, so anything it guessed at can be corrected afterwards.

exp: The gap is that you do not yet know what you left out, and an interview is the cheapest way to find out — it asks about invalidation before anything is committed to. Writing a fuller specification is the strongest alternative and works when you already know the concerns, which is the thing missing here. Reviewing afterwards spends a whole implementation cycle to learn the same list.

q: A CI step runs `claude "Refactor the deprecated logger calls in this diff"` and the job stalls until it times out, never producing output. What's the correct fix?

choices.t: Set an environment variable like CLAUDE_CI=1 before the command so Claude detects the pipeline and skips its interactive prompt.
Wrap the command with a shell timeout and a retry loop so a stalled run is killed and re-attempted until one of them returns.
Add the -p (--print) flag so Claude runs non-interactively: it processes the prompt, prints the result to stdout, and exits.
Append --no-interactive to the invocation so Claude bypasses the interactive session and emits the refactor result directly.

exp: Without -p, the CLI starts an interactive session and waits for input, which hangs in CI. The -p/--print flag runs non-interactively — process, print, exit. CLAUDE_CI and --no-interactive aren't real features, and wrapping a stalled command in timeouts and retries treats the symptom instead of using the correct invocation.

q: You are iterating on a date-range parser, and each round fixes one edge case while quietly breaking another — open-ended ranges, inclusive versus exclusive bounds. What most reliably anchors the iteration?

choices.t: Write a test set covering the edge cases and expected bounds up front, then iterate by running it and fixing failures.
Have Claude generate the test set alongside the parser, then iterate against those tests as the specification.
Regenerate the parser from scratch each round rather than patching, so newly introduced regressions do not accumulate.
List the edge cases in the prompt and ask it to reason through each one before writing the next version of the parser.

exp: Regressions keep slipping through because nothing re-checks the earlier cases; a test set written first turns every round into a measurable pass or fail. Having Claude write the tests is the strongest alternative and produces a harness quickly — but tests derived from the same understanding that produced the bug encode the same blind spot on the very cases in dispute.

q: Context is nearly full during a migration, so you plan to run /compact. You're worried about losing the exact version pins and file paths Claude discovered. What protects them through the compaction?

choices.t: Skip /compact and just raise max_tokens instead, so the full discovery history stays intact and nothing needs protecting.
Persist the version pins and paths into a facts block (or scratchpad) kept outside the history, then run /compact.
Run /compact first and then ask Claude to recall the exact pins and paths from the summary it just produced for the session.
Run /compact repeatedly so the summary keeps getting tighter, which forces the model to retain only the most exact details.

exp: /compact summarizes history to free the window, but exact numbers, dates, and paths are precisely what summarization condenses into vague text. Writing them to a facts block or scratchpad outside the summarized history preserves them. Larger max_tokens just delays the limit, and recalling from a summary that already dropped the details — or compacting harder — loses more, not less.

q: A code-intelligence tool returns 40+ metadata fields per symbol, but your rename refactor only needs the name, file, and line. Over a long session this output piles up and recall degrades. Best fix?

choices.t: Trim the tool output to name, file, and line before it enters context, so the unused fields never accumulate at all.
Summarize the accumulated symbol metadata every few turns, keeping the history compact as the refactor proceeds.
Raise max_tokens so all forty fields per symbol fit, letting the model hold the full payload without dropping any.
Store the full symbol payloads in CLAUDE.md, keeping them out of the chat while still available on every request.

exp: The noise is created at the source, so filtering the tool output before it lands is what actually stops the accumulation. Periodic summarization is the strongest alternative and does slow the growth — but it compresses the very identifiers the rename depends on. A larger budget fills with the same noise, and CLAUDE.md is loaded on every request.

q: Each subagent returns clean output, but the final report sometimes contradicts itself because two search agents pulled overlapping facts that differ slightly and nothing reconciled them. Whose responsibility is that reconciliation?

choices.t: The coordinator's: aggregating and validating subagent results before synthesis is what the hub role exists to do.
The synthesis agent's, since it is the first stage that sees all the findings together and could reconcile there.
Each subagent's, since whichever runs last can read the others' outputs and settle facts that disagree with its own.
Nobody's in particular: independent search agents will occasionally disagree, and a note in the report covers it.

exp: In a hub-and-spoke system the coordinator is the only component that sees every result, so validating them against each other before synthesis is its job. Synthesis is the strongest alternative and does see everything — but by then the contradiction is an input to writing rather than a fact to resolve, and it cannot re-query a source. Subagents cannot read each other's output at all.

q: A coordinator spawns the document-analysis subagent with the Task prompt “Analyze the document” and gets vague, ungrounded output. What must a well-formed Task prompt for this subagent contain?

choices.t: The document text, the relevant prior search results, and the required output format, all supplied in the prompt itself.
The document text and the required output format, leaving the prior search results out to keep the subagent focused.
A reference to the document by filename, which the subagent resolves and reads before starting its analysis.
The coordinator's session identifier, which the subagent uses to replay the conversation and recover the document.

exp: A subagent begins with nothing but its prompt, so everything it must reason over goes in: the text, the prior findings that give it context, and the shape of the answer. Sending the text and format but omitting the search results is the strongest alternative and is right when the analysis is genuinely standalone — here that missing grounding is the vagueness.

q: For a broad topic the coordinator spawns four search subagents, but their results overlap heavily — three of them surfaced largely the same sources — while other angles stay uncovered. What decomposition change helps most?

choices.t: Have the coordinator assign each subagent a distinct, non-overlapping slice of the topic so coverage divides cleanly.
Have each subagent declare its intended angle first, so the coordinator can reject one overlapping an earlier claim.
Reduce to a single search subagent covering the whole topic, removing the overlap along with the parallelism.
Keep the four agents and raise each one's result count, so distinct sources appear alongside the duplicated ones.

exp: Overlap is a decomposition problem, so the coordinator fixes it where the subtasks are defined: distinct slices, assigned up front. Having agents declare angles is the strongest alternative and would catch collisions — but it adds a negotiation round for something the coordinator already knows when it partitions. Collapsing to one agent trades overlap for lost breadth.

q: The report-generation agent's output is handed to a stakeholder who never sees the pipeline, the sources, or any intermediate agent output. What property must that final report have to be useful?

choices.t: It must be complete and self-contained, carrying the findings, source attributions, and conclusions the reader needs in one place.
It must be as short as possible, since a stakeholder will trust a brief summary more than a detailed report with cited findings and caveats.
It must embed the raw tool outputs and full reasoning traces from every subagent, so the stakeholder can audit each step the pipeline took.
It must link back to each subagent's live session so the stakeholder can open them and inspect the underlying search and analysis context.

exp: Like a structured escalation handoff, a final report goes to someone with no access to the pipeline, so it must be self-contained: findings, attribution, and conclusions in one place. Raw traces or links to agent sessions push the work back onto a reader who can't reach that context, and over-trimming drops the substance.

q: To “give each subagent every advantage,” a developer passes the coordinator's entire accumulated conversation into every Task prompt. Subagents get slower and occasionally act on irrelevant earlier findings. What is the better practice?

choices.t: Send each subagent only its task and the data that task needs, keeping its context focused on the assigned slice.
Compress the accumulated history into a short briefing and pass that, so prior context is present without the volume.
Keep passing the full history but instruct each subagent to ignore whatever is not relevant to its assignment.
Pass no context at all and let each subagent rediscover what it needs through its own tool calls during the run.

exp: A subagent's context should be scoped to its task: irrelevant findings are both cost and a source of off-task actions. Compressing the history is the strongest alternative and cuts the volume — but it still hands every agent the other agents' work, so the irrelevance survives in shorter form. Telling a model to ignore context is not a filter, and passing nothing starves it.

q: One subtopic ends up thinly covered because its search agent timed out, and re-running it before the deadline is not possible. How should synthesis present that section?

choices.t: Include the partial findings and annotate the section as limited coverage, naming the timeout that caused the gap.
Include the partial findings and annotate them as limited, without attributing the gap to a specific internal failure.
Present the partial findings formatted like the rest, so the report reads consistently across all of its sections.
Omit the subtopic entirely, since a section built on incomplete evidence invites more doubt than it resolves.

exp: When a gap cannot be closed, the honest form is partial findings plus an explicit coverage note, and naming the cause tells the reader whether the thinness reflects the literature or the run. Annotating without the cause is the strongest alternative and is defensible for an external audience — it just leaves the reader unable to tell a sparse field from a failed search.

q: To cut a hop, a developer wires the web-search and document-analysis subagents to send their results straight to the report-writing agent instead of back to the coordinator. Integration quality drops. Why?

choices.t: The report-writing agent can only accept input from one upstream subagent at a time, so the second agent's results are dropped on arrival.
Centralized integration is lost: the coordinator should collect both result sets and pass them to synthesis for a unified merge.
Direct subagent-to-subagent messaging is blocked by the Task tool, so the results never actually reach the report-writing agent at all.
The report-writing agent needs fork_session to merge two upstream branches, and without it the two result sets can't be combined.

exp: In a hub-and-spoke design the coordinator forwards both result sets to the synthesis/report step for a centralized, high-quality merge; bypassing it forfeits that control. The other options invent technical blockers — fork_session isn't a merge mechanism, and Task doesn't forbid the data flow; the real cost is losing coordinator-mediated integration.

q: Mid-run, one of five subagents fails unrecoverably. The coordinator currently aborts the whole job and discards the four completed sections. What is the better orchestration behavior?

choices.t: Keep the four completed sections, proceed to a report, and annotate the missing section as a gap caused by the failure.
Retry the failed subagent once, and if it fails again proceed with the four sections and the gap annotated.
Abort as it does now but restart the pipeline automatically, so the report is always built from a fully successful run.
Keep the four sections and present the report without reference to the fifth, so the output reads as complete.

exp: Four usable sections are worth more than none, so the coordinator degrades gracefully and marks what is missing. Retrying once first is the strongest alternative and is often the better policy — but the question is what to do with the completed work, and a retry that also fails lands back on exactly this choice. Restarting discards four good sections.

q: Your search subagents are configured with the coordinator's full toolset (search, analysis, synthesis, report). They sometimes drift into analysis instead of searching, and their context fills up. What is the most direct fix?

choices.t: Restrict each subagent's allowedTools to the tools its role needs, which removes the off-task options entirely.
Give each subagent a role-specific system prompt describing its boundaries, alongside the shared toolset it has.
Have the coordinator reject any subagent result produced by a tool outside that subagent's assigned role.
Raise each subagent's context budget so the unused tool definitions no longer crowd out its search results.

exp: Scoping allowedTools removes the off-task tools from the model's choices, fixing the drift and the definitions bloating context in one move. A role-specific prompt is the strongest alternative and does state the boundary — but the tools stay callable, so the constraint is advisory. Rejecting results afterwards wastes the work that was already done.

q: Each specialized subagent (search, analysis, synthesis) is provisioned with the union of all four roles' tools “for flexibility,” and selection reliability across the system drops. What is the sound allocation principle?

choices.t: Give each subagent its role-relevant tools plus the few shared utilities it genuinely needs, and nothing beyond that.
Give each subagent its role's tools and let it request another through the coordinator when a task genuinely needs one.
Keep the union but force each subagent's first call with tool_choice, so its opening action is always role-appropriate.
Keep the union but describe each role's permitted subset in that subagent's system prompt, leaving the tools in place.

exp: Selection reliability falls as the candidate set grows, so each role gets what it needs and no more. Escalating through the coordinator is the strongest alternative and is sound for genuinely occasional needs — it just adds a round-trip where a small set of shared utilities would do. Forcing the first call leaves every later turn over-provisioned.

q: The document-analysis subagent fails differently per file: some PDFs are corrupted, some are password-protected, some are empty. Today every failure returns “could not process.” What should it return instead?

choices.t: A structured error carrying a failure_type — corrupted, permission, or empty — plus a readable message for the coordinator.
A structured error carrying the underlying library exception, from which the coordinator can infer the category.
The same message for all three, with the per-file detail written to a log the operator reviews after the run.
A partial success for every file, with the failure reason recorded in the result metadata for later inspection.

exp: Three failures need three responses — skip it, request a password, note the empty file — so the type must be a field the coordinator can branch on. Returning the raw exception is the strongest alternative and does carry the information, but it makes the coordinator parse library-specific strings that change when the parser is upgraded. A log is not visible to the run in progress.

q: Your search subagent is supposed to always invoke one of its search tools, but it occasionally answers from its own prior knowledge in plain text instead of searching. Which setting guarantees it calls a tool?

choices.t: Leave tool_choice on "auto" and strengthen the prompt to insist the subagent must always run a real search before answering anything.
Set tool_choice to "any", which forces the subagent to call one of its tools while still letting it choose which search tool fits.
Pin tool_choice to one specific search tool so the subagent is locked to that single tool for every query type it ever receives.
Remove every non-search tool from the subagent so the only remaining option is a search tool, even though text replies stay allowed.

exp: tool_choice "any" guarantees a tool call while leaving the model free to pick the right search tool. "auto" still permits a text answer no matter how forceful the prompt; pinning one tool ignores query variety; and removing other tools doesn't stop the model from replying in text rather than searching.

q: A search subagent retries a flaky upstream endpoint indefinitely on transient errors, so one slow source can stall the whole research run for minutes. What is the right local-recovery policy?

choices.t: Attempt one or two local retries, then propagate a structured error carrying whatever partial results were gathered.
Propagate the first transient error immediately with partial results, leaving all retry policy to the coordinator.
Keep retrying until the endpoint responds, since a transient error means the data exists and will return shortly.
Treat the transient error as terminal and return a non-retryable status, so no further attempt is made anywhere.

exp: A brief flake is cheapest to absorb where it happened, so the subagent retries once or twice and then hands up a structured error with what it has. Delegating all retry policy to the coordinator is the strongest alternative and does centralize the decision — but it spends a full round-trip on a failure that usually clears on the second attempt.

q: The synthesis subagent occasionally needs to re-fetch a single cited page to confirm a quote, but giving it the search agent's full browse/crawl toolset led to it going off on tangents. Best scoping?

choices.t: Give synthesis a narrow tool that fetches one already-cited URL, leaving broad browsing with the search agent.
Give synthesis the search agent's full browsing toolset, so it can re-check any page it needs during synthesis.
Give synthesis no fetch capability and have the search agent attach the full text of every cited page to its findings.
Share one broad fetch tool between the search and synthesis agents, so there is a single implementation to maintain.

exp: Match the tool to the role's actual need: re-reading a page that is already cited is a narrow operation and does not require crawl capability. Attaching every cited page up front is the strongest alternative and removes the need entirely — but it inflates every finding with text that synthesis usually will not open.

q: Across a long research run, whichever subagent runs last tends to have its context crowded with verbose outputs from earlier, unrelated subagents. Which architectural role prevents that leakage?

choices.t: The coordinator as a separate context layer, aggregating outputs and giving each subagent only what its task requires.
A shared store the subagents read from and write to, so each one pulls only the entries its own task refers to.
A summarization step between subagents, condensing each output before it is carried into the next one's context.
A larger context window on every subagent, so the accumulated prior outputs no longer crowd out the current task.

exp: The coordinator holds the aggregated state and hands each subagent a scoped slice, so one agent's output never lands in another's window. A shared store is the strongest alternative and can work — but it makes every subagent responsible for its own filtering, and unfiltered reading is precisely the failure described. Summarizing shrinks the leak rather than stopping it.

q: A long multi-agent research run crashes after the search and analysis agents finish but before synthesis. On restart the coordinator redoes everything from zero. What design enables resuming without re-running completed work?

choices.t: Rely on a session resume to automatically restore every agent's in-memory state, so the run simply continues from the crash point untouched.
Have each agent persist structured state to a known location and load a manifest on restart to re-inject completed work.
Keep all agent state only in the coordinator's live context window, trusting it to survive the crash and be read back after the restart.
Accept the full re-run as the cost of recovery, since a crash always means the research job must be repeated from the beginning.

exp: Durable, structured state exports plus a manifest the coordinator reads on restart let it skip the search and analysis steps and resume at synthesis. In-memory or live-context state doesn't survive a crash, and treating every crash as a full re-run discards the completed search and analysis work.

q: Your loop issues two tool calls in one assistant turn, runs both, and sends the results back. The API rejects the request. What must the next user message contain?

choices.t: One tool_result block for each tool_use id from that turn, returned together in the same user message.
The two tool_result blocks in two consecutive user messages, one per call, in the order they were issued.
A single tool_result block combining both outputs, since they were produced within the same assistant turn.
The tool_result blocks plus a restatement of the original request, so the model can re-anchor on the task.

exp: Every tool_use block must be answered by a tool_result carrying the matching id, and all of them belong in the one user message replying to that turn. Splitting them across messages is the strongest alternative and does preserve the ids — but it leaves the first message answering only part of the turn, which is what the API rejects.

q: A teammate's exploration agent maps a service by running Glob across the whole repo, then Reading every matched file in alphabetical order before answering any question. It is slow and frequently runs out of context. What is the core flaw?

choices.t: It reads exhaustively before knowing what matters, spending the context budget ahead of any question.
Alphabetical order confuses the model; sorting the matched files by size would let it finish in time.
Glob is the wrong discovery tool, and only a recursive Bash listing enumerates the files reliably.
The context window is too small for the approach, which is otherwise sound once nothing is truncated.

exp: The flaw is the strategy rather than its parameters: reading every file front-loads the entire cost before the agent knows which files bear on the question. Ordering and window size change how far it gets before running out, not whether the approach scales at all.

q: Task: "Find why checkout intermittently double-charges and fix it." The root cause is unknown and could span the payment, retry, or queue layers. Which decomposition strategy fits best?

choices.t: Run a fixed prompt-chained pipeline that reviews payment, then retry, then queue code in a set order on every run.
Map the involved layers, follow the evidence, and adapt the plan as each finding narrows where the fault lives.
Send one large prompt asking the model to read all three layers at once and return the bug along with a fix in a single pass.
Split the work into three independent subagents that each rewrite one layer in parallel without sharing what they find.

exp: An open-ended root-cause hunt suits adaptive decomposition that re-plans as evidence accumulates. A fixed pipeline assumes a known structure, a single giant prompt dilutes attention, and parallel rewrites without shared findings risk three uncoordinated changes to an unconfirmed cause.

q: You investigated an auth bug last week in a named session, and the auth files have been heavily refactored since. A teammate suggests resuming it and running /compact first. Does that address the problem?

choices.t: No — /compact summarizes the existing history, so the stale tool results are condensed rather than refreshed.
Yes — /compact re-runs the cached tool calls while summarizing, so the results match the refactored files.
Yes — /compact drops tool results entirely, leaving only conclusions that remain valid after the refactor.
No — but only because /compact is unavailable in a resumed session, so the history cannot be trimmed there.

exp: /compact shortens the conversation; it does not re-execute anything, so a stale file listing simply becomes a shorter stale file listing. The fix is a fresh read of the changed files, either in a new session or by telling the resumed one what moved. Both yes answers credit /compact with refreshing data it never touches.

q: After a deep exploration of a legacy service, you want to prototype a Redux migration and a Context-API migration that both start from that exact analysis, comparing them without re-running discovery. Best mechanism?

choices.t: Start two fresh sessions and re-paste the legacy service into each so both prototypes begin from the same analysis.
Use fork_session to branch two independent sessions from the shared analysis baseline, then let each diverge.
Run --resume on the one named session twice in parallel and keep the two migrations' state from colliding by hand.
Stay in one session, /compact the analysis, and ask for both migration prototypes within that single thread.

exp: fork_session branches independent explorations from a shared baseline, so both inherit the analysis then diverge cleanly. Fresh sessions discard the analysis, resuming one session twice collides shared state, and one compacted thread can't keep the two prototypes isolated for comparison.

q: An engineer asks the agent to “explain how requests flow through this framework.” It answers from the framework's name alone, never opening a file, and gets the wiring wrong. What most reliably grounds the next attempt?

choices.t: Require the explanation to cite the file and line for each hop, so every claim is tied to code it actually opened.
Name the entry point yourself and ask it to trace outward from there, following the imports that it finds.
Tell it not to rely on general knowledge of similar frameworks when describing this one's request flow.
Ask the same question again and keep whichever explanation of the request flow comes back most often.

exp: Requiring a citation per hop makes the answer falsifiable and forces the agent into the files, because an uncited claim is visibly unsupported. Naming the entry point is the strongest alternative and does start it in the right place — but nothing then stops it from filling the later hops from memory, which is the failure described.

q: Your Grep for API_BASE_URL returns 400 matches, most of them inside generated bundles and vendored dependencies. What is the most effective next step?

choices.t: Re-run the Grep scoped to the source directories, excluding the generated and vendored paths from the search.
Pipe the same Grep through a second filter that drops any result whose path contains a build or vendor segment.
Read the matched files in order until the genuine references are found, skipping the generated ones by eye.
Switch to Glob to list the source files first, then open each one looking for the variable by hand.

exp: The search is right and its scope is wrong, so constrain the scope: restricting Grep to the source paths removes the noise before it is ever returned. Filtering the output afterwards is the strongest alternative and reaches the same set — it just pays to search and transfer 400 matches in order to discard most of them.

q: Your team's shared GitHub MCP server is configured in project .mcp.json with "env": {"GITHUB_TOKEN": "${GITHUB_TOKEN}"}. A new teammate connects and the server fails to authenticate, though the file is identical to everyone else's. Most likely cause?

choices.t: The .mcp.json must hard-code the literal token value instead, because environment-variable expansion is not supported in that file.
The shared GitHub server belongs in each teammate's ~/.claude.json, not in the version-controlled project .mcp.json.
The teammate hasn't set the GITHUB_TOKEN variable in their environment, so the ${GITHUB_TOKEN} reference expands to nothing.
CLAUDE.md is missing a line documenting the token, which is what actually supplies the value the server reads at startup.

exp: Env-var expansion in .mcp.json keeps tokens out of version control, but each developer must supply the variable in their own environment; an unset GITHUB_TOKEN expands to empty and auth fails. Hard-coding the token leaks it, the shared server correctly lives in project .mcp.json, and CLAUDE.md is context, not server configuration.

q: To "cover every workflow," a teammate connects nine MCP servers to the dev agent, exposing 70+ tools at once. The agent now misroutes simple file edits to unrelated tools. Why does this happen, and what's the fix?

choices.t: Tools from all connected servers are exposed together, so 70+ choices degrade selection; connect only the servers the task needs.
Each connected server overrides the previous one's tools, so only the last server's tools work; reorder the servers in .mcp.json to fix it.
The servers must each be namespaced by hand before connecting, since identical tool names across servers are what causes the misrouting here.
Nine servers exceed the connection limit, so some fail silently; raise the limit and the agent will route every simple edit correctly again.

exp: On connection, every server's tools are discovered and made available simultaneously, so 70+ tools inflate the model's selection space and reliability drops — the fix is connecting only the servers a task needs. Servers don't override each other, manual namespacing isn't the cause, and there is no connection cap doing this.

q: You're trialing an experimental MCP server you wrote over the weekend. It isn't ready for the team and you don't want it landing in everyone's setup, but you need it for your own work. Where should you register it?

choices.t: In your user-level ~/.claude.json, which keeps the experimental server off your teammates' setups entirely.
In the project's committed .mcp.json, where every MCP server the repo uses is expected to be declared.
In a .mcp.local.json alongside .mcp.json, the file reserved for uncommitted experimental servers.
As a documented block in the project CLAUDE.md, describing the server so that only you start it manually.

exp: User-scoped configuration is per-machine and unversioned, which is exactly the isolation an unfinished server needs. The project file would push it to everyone on the next pull, CLAUDE.md carries context rather than server configuration, and there is no .mcp.local.json mechanism.

q: You must migrate 50+ files off a deprecated logging library, and you have already chosen the wiring approach. What is the soundest way to execute the migration?

choices.t: Migrate one representative file first, verify it end to end, then apply the confirmed pattern across the rest.
Migrate the files in small batches, reviewing each batch before starting the next one across the service.
Migrate all 50+ files in one pass, then run the full test suite once to catch whatever the change broke.
Migrate the files individually, with a separate approval step written up before each one is edited.

exp: A pilot file proves the pattern where a mistake is cheap to unwind, and the rest then follow a verified template. Small batches are the strongest alternative and are the right shape once the pattern is proven — starting there means a flaw in the approach surfaces after several files rather than one. One giant pass makes the failure hardest to diagnose.

q: Your repo has a root CLAUDE.md requiring camelCase, and packages/legacy-api has its own CLAUDE.md requiring snake_case. An engineer edits a file inside packages/legacy-api. What applies?

choices.t: Both load, with the directory-level file taking precedence wherever the two give conflicting instructions.
Both load, and the model reconciles the conflict from context, since neither file declares a precedence.
Only the directory-level CLAUDE.md loads, since the nearest file replaces the root one for that subtree.
Only the root CLAUDE.md loads, since project-wide conventions are not overridden by nested files.

exp: CLAUDE.md files compose from the root down, and the most specific one wins where they disagree — which is what makes a per-directory override useful at all. Leaving the conflict to the model is the strongest alternative and describes a real risk when two files disagree implicitly, but an explicit nested convention is designed to take precedence.

q: Your CI review prompt already works, but findings come back as narrative paragraphs a script must hand-copy into PR comments. You want each finding posted as an inline comment with file, line, and severity. Best approach?

choices.t: Add an "Output Format" section to CLAUDE.md with sample findings so Claude learns the expected layout from project context.
Run the review with --output-format json and --json-schema, then parse the structured output to post each inline comment.
Keep the narrative output and add a second Claude call whose job is to summarize the findings into a JSON object afterward.
Add a prompt instruction requiring each finding to follow a template like [FILE:path][LINE:n][SEVERITY:level] for parsing.

exp: Enforcing structure at the CLI level with --output-format json plus --json-schema guarantees well-formed fields a script can reliably parse and post. A CLAUDE.md section, a delimiter template, or a second summarizing call all still rely on the model formatting prose consistently, which it won't.

q: Every CI run re-states your review rules in the prompt, and the wording drifts between jobs. You want one source of review criteria for all CI-triggered runs. Where does it belong?

choices.t: Committed to the project CLAUDE.md, which loads as project context for every CI-triggered Claude Code run.
In a version-controlled prompt file the pipeline reads and passes in, so each job sends identical wording.
Hard-coded into each pipeline job definition, so the rules travel alongside the CI configuration itself.
Passed as a --json-schema argument on every invocation, so the schema doubles as the review rulebook.

exp: Project CLAUDE.md is version-controlled context that loads automatically wherever the repo is checked out, so every job gets identical criteria without any job doing anything. A shared prompt file is the strongest alternative and is equally versioned — it just needs each pipeline to remember to read and pass it, which is the drift you are removing.

q: Your CI step asks Claude to suggest tests for each PR. On one it proposes ten, and six duplicate scenarios the existing suite already covers. What most effectively reduces the duplication?

choices.t: Include the module's existing test file in context, so Claude can see which scenarios are already covered.
Add a post-processing step that drops a suggestion when its description matches an existing test name.
Ask for five suggestions instead of ten, so the model has to choose which scenarios are worth proposing.
Ask for edge cases and error conditions only, leaving the happy-path scenarios to the existing suite.

exp: The model cannot avoid re-proposing what it cannot see, so the existing tests belong in context. Post-processing is the strongest alternative and catches the obvious repeats — but it matches on names, so a duplicate scenario worded differently survives, and it spends generation on suggestions it then discards. Asking for fewer does not make the rest novel.

q: A teammate writes a CI step as `claude -p "Review this PR" > review.txt`, expecting JSON, then complains the file holds prose. They want machine-readable findings AND the job to keep exiting on its own. What's the accurate fix?

choices.t: The -p flag both runs non-interactively and emits JSON, so the real bug is the redirection truncating the structured output.
-p only makes the run non-interactive and prints to stdout; add --output-format json (with --json-schema) to get parseable findings.
Replace -p with --output-format json, since that flag is what runs Claude non-interactively and prints structured findings to stdout.
Keep -p and pipe the prose through a JSON-wrapping shell script, because the CLI cannot emit structured findings on its own.

exp: -p (--print) only controls non-interactive execution and prints to stdout; it does not change the format, which is prose by default. Structured findings require --output-format json, ideally with --json-schema. -p and --output-format are separate flags serving different jobs, and the CLI does emit JSON natively, so a wrapper is unnecessary.

q: Tests generated in CI compile but hand-roll their setup, ignoring the fixtures and helpers your project already provides. What most directly gets generated tests onto the existing harness?

choices.t: Include one existing test that already uses the fixtures as an exemplar in the generation prompt.
Document the available fixtures and testing standards in CLAUDE.md so every run carries them as context.
Add a prompt line instructing the model to reuse the project's existing helpers wherever they apply.
Run the generation against the whole test directory so the model can discover the fixtures for itself.

exp: An exemplar shows the harness in use — the imports, the fixture names, the setup call — which is what the model reproduces. Documenting the fixtures in CLAUDE.md is the strongest alternative and is worth doing anyway, but a prose inventory still leaves the model inferring how the pieces fit together, and that inference is where hand-rolled setup comes from.

q: Your pipeline runs one Claude Code session that generates fix suggestions and then reviews them before posting. You have decided the review must be independent. How should the CI steps be arranged?

choices.t: A second claude -p invocation receiving the generated diff as its input, knowing nothing of how it was produced.
A second claude -p invocation receiving the diff along with the generation transcript, for the fuller context.
The same session, with the review turn issued after a /compact that trims the generation reasoning away.
Two parallel invocations that each generate and review, with the pipeline posting whichever pair agrees.

exp: Independence means the reviewer does not hold the reasoning that produced the code, so it receives the diff and nothing else. Passing the transcript too is the strongest alternative and gives richer context — but it hands back the justifications whose absence is the entire point. Compaction condenses that reasoning rather than removing it.

q: Your review prompt says “check that comments are accurate.” It flags acceptable TODO markers while missing comments describing behavior the code no longer has. Which change best fixes the inconsistency?

choices.t: Specify the rule explicitly: flag a comment only where what it claims contradicts what the code actually does.
Attach git blame so the reviewer can weigh comments that predate the most recent change to the code.
Pre-filter TODO and FIXME markers out of the diff, so only descriptive comments reach the reviewer at all.
Add a line asking it to be conservative and report only high-confidence comment problems in its output.

exp: “Accurate” is doing no work in the prompt, so the fix names the test the reviewer should apply: a contradiction between what the comment claims and what the code does. Git blame is the strongest alternative and is genuine evidence — but age is not inaccuracy, and a comment written yesterday can already be wrong.

q: Your reviews surface real bugs, but the wording is unactionable — “complex routing logic,” “potential null pointer,” with no fix. Adding “always include a concrete fix” has not made the output consistent. What most reliably fixes the shape?

choices.t: Provide three or four examples showing the exact shape of a finding: the issue, its location, and a suggested fix.
Require each finding to be returned as a schema with issue, location, and fix as separate required fields.
Expand the instruction to spell out each part a finding must contain before the model writes it out.
Split it into two passes, one identifying the issues and a second writing a fix for each one found.

exp: Instructions describe a format; examples demonstrate it, which is why few-shot pins down a shape that prose keeps missing. A required schema is the strongest alternative and does guarantee the fields exist — it just cannot make the fix field hold something concrete rather than a restatement of the issue.

q: Your bot rates similar null-pointer risks “critical” on one PR and “medium” on another, so developers cannot trust the severities. You have already told it to assign appropriate severity. What most improves consistency?

choices.t: Define each severity level with a concrete example, such as critical meaning a crash on a user-facing payment path.
Collapse the scale to blocking and non-blocking, so there are fewer levels for the ratings to disagree about.
Include the severities assigned on recent pull requests, so new ratings are anchored to that precedent.
Have the model rate its confidence per finding and map higher confidence onto a higher severity label.

exp: Ratings drift because “appropriate” is undefined, so anchoring each level to a concrete example gives the model a fixed rubric to match against. Collapsing the scale is the strongest alternative and does raise agreement — by discarding the triage information the levels existed to carry. Precedent anchors to whatever drift already happened.

q: Your review step is iterative: Claude analyzes the changed file, then calls a tool to fetch related files (imports, base classes) before finalizing feedback. A manager wants it on the Batch API for 50% savings. What's the blocking limitation?

choices.t: The Batch API can't attach correlation IDs, so findings couldn't be mapped back to the pull request that produced them.
The Batch API rejects tool definitions in request parameters, so the file-fetching tool could never be declared in the first place.
The asynchronous batch model can't run a tool mid-request and feed results back for Claude to continue its analysis.
Batch latency of up to 24 hours is too slow for PR feedback, though the iterative tool-calling itself would still function.

exp: Batch is fire-and-forget—one request, one response—so it can't pause to execute a tool and return its output for Claude to keep reasoning, which this multi-round workflow requires. custom_id does provide correlation, tool definitions are accepted, and latency is a separate concern from the fundamental inability to do mid-request tool calls.

q: Your CI runs three analyses: fast style checks that block merge, weekly full-repo security audits, and nightly test generation for changed modules. You want the 50% batch savings without hurting developer experience. Which mapping is right?

choices.t: Use batch for all three and have the pipeline poll for completion, accepting the wait everywhere to maximize the savings.
Use synchronous calls for style checks and nightly test generation; reserve the Batch API only for the weekly security audit.
Use synchronous calls for the blocking style checks; use the Batch API for the security audits and the nightly test generation.
Use synchronous calls for all three to keep latency uniform, and rely on prompt caching to claw back most of the cost difference instead.

exp: Only the style checks block a waiting developer and need synchronous latency; the weekly audit and nightly test generation are scheduled jobs that tolerate the up-to-24-hour batch window, so both capture the 50% savings. Batching the blocking check stalls merges, and keeping all three synchronous forgoes savings that two of them could safely take.

q: To analyze false positives, you want to know which code pattern triggered each finding so you can spot the recurring noisy ones. The findings currently carry only an issue description and severity. What schema change enables this?

choices.t: Add a detected_pattern field to each finding, recording the rule that fired so noisy patterns can be aggregated.
Append a free-text rationale to each finding and read through them periodically to spot recurring triggers.
Group the findings by file and severity, so the categories producing the most noise stand out in the report.
Record the prompt version alongside each finding, so noise can be traced to the wording that produced it.

exp: Aggregating by trigger requires the trigger to be a field, so detected_pattern turns the analysis into a group-by rather than a reading exercise. A free-text rationale is the strongest alternative and carries the same information — but it is not comparable across findings, so counting the recurring ones stays manual.

q: With limited reviewer time, you want the bot to route only its riskiest findings to a human while auto-posting the rest. The current output is a flat list with no risk signal. Which design best supports calibrated routing?

choices.t: Send the human every finding on PRs that touch the most files, treating raw PR size as the proxy for which reviews are risky.
Trust the model's prose claims like "I'm confident this is a real bug" and route to a human only when it says it is unsure.
Have the bot emit a calibrated confidence per finding and route the low-confidence or contradictory ones to human review.
Route a fixed random 10% of all findings to the human regardless of how certain or uncertain the model was about each one.

exp: A calibrated per-finding confidence lets a verification pass send exactly the uncertain or contradictory findings to scarce reviewers while auto-handling the rest. PR size is a weak risk proxy, uncalibrated prose self-assessments are unreliable, and a flat random sample ignores risk entirely—reviewing safe findings and missing dangerous ones.

q: Your schema-valid extractions store dates and currencies, but values arrive inconsistently — “yesterday,” “five bucks,” “half.” What best normalizes them?

choices.t: State the normalization rules in the prompt: ISO 8601 dates, a numeric amount plus currency code, decimals for percentages.
Add a normalization layer after extraction that rewrites the freeform dates and amounts into canonical form.
Tighten the schema field types so the tool_use call rejects any value that is not already normalized.
Add examples of correctly normalized values for each field, so the model matches the shape it is shown.

exp: The values are valid but inconsistent, a semantic problem, so the rules belong where the model applies them as it extracts. A post-extraction normalizer is the strongest alternative and is worth having as a backstop — but it must interpret “half” without the surrounding document, which is the context that made the value readable. A stricter type rejects rather than converts.

q: Your pipeline must always run extract_metadata first, so enrichment has a document type before any other tool is considered. Which tool_choice setting enforces that first step?

choices.t: Forced selection: tool_choice {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"}, which guarantees that exact tool runs.
tool_choice "any" on the first turn with only extract_metadata supplied, adding the other tools afterwards.
tool_choice "any", which forces a tool call and leaves the model to pick extract_metadata from the set.
tool_choice "auto" plus a prompt line instructing the model to call extract_metadata before anything else.

exp: Naming the tool is the only setting that guarantees which tool runs; the others guarantee at most that some tool runs. Restricting the first turn to a single tool is the strongest alternative and reaches the same outcome — it just gets there by editing the tool list per turn rather than stating the constraint, which is more moving parts for one guarantee.

q: tool_use guarantees your extracted JSON parses and matches the declared field types, yet contracts whose start_date falls after end_date still pass. Where should that rule live?

choices.t: In a custom validator run after parsing, enforcing the relationship that start_date must precede end_date.
In the extraction prompt, stating the constraint so the model does not emit an inverted pair to begin with.
In the JSON schema, as a constraint comparing the two fields so tool_use rejects the inverted ordering.
Nowhere: ordering between two typed date fields is a syntax concern a strict schema already blocks.

exp: Cross-field relationships are semantic, and a schema validates each field's type and presence rather than how two of them relate, so the rule belongs in a validator after parsing. Stating it in the prompt is the strongest alternative and is worth doing as well — it makes a violation less likely without making it impossible.

q: When deciding whether to mark an extraction field as required in the schema, what is the governing principle for avoiding fabricated values?

choices.t: Mark a field required only where the information is reliably present, since a required field pushes the model to invent one.
Mark every field required and let a validation layer reject the records where a value was clearly fabricated.
Mark fields required based on how much downstream consumers depend on them being populated in each record.
Treat requiredness as advisory, since tool_use returns every declared field whether or not it is marked required.

exp: Requiredness is a statement about the source rather than about how much you want the value: a field the document may not contain forces a fabrication once it is marked required. Choosing by downstream need is the strongest alternative and is a real consideration — but it is exactly the reasoning that produces required fields the source cannot support.

q: Recipe documents describe quantities informally ("two handfuls of rice", "a pinch of salt") that no fixed rule set captures well. Best extraction technique?

choices.t: Provide a few few-shot examples mapping informal phrases to amount, original_text, and a precision marker like approximate.
Write an exhaustive rule list mapping every informal phrase you can think of to a precise gram value in the prompt itself.
Reject any document that contains non-standard units so that only recipes with metric measurements ever reach the extractor.
Constrain the amount field to an integer enum of common gram values so the informal phrases snap to the nearest listed one.

exp: Few-shot examples are especially effective for informal, diverse units that defy rule-based instructions; they let the model generalize while tagging precision. An exhaustive rule list cannot cover the variety, and rejecting documents or forcing an integer enum loses data.

q: An invoice extraction fails validation because the stated total does not match the summed line items. For an effective retry, the follow-up prompt should include which content?

choices.t: The original document, the previous extraction, and the specific error naming the mismatched total and the sum.
The previous extraction and the specific error, since the model still holds the document from the earlier turn.
A fresh copy of the document alone, so the model re-extracts without being anchored to its earlier attempt.
The schema and a reminder that the line items must reconcile to the stated total before it responds again.

exp: An effective retry gives the model the source, its own previous answer, and the concrete discrepancy, so it can find what it read wrong. Omitting the document is the strongest alternative and would be right in a stateful session — but each API call carries only what you send, so the earlier turn's document is not there unless it is resent.

q: Some documents genuinely do not make a category obvious, and the model currently guesses, producing confident but wrong labels. Which schema design reduces that?

choices.t: Add an "unclear" value to the category enum, so the model can decline rather than force a wrong label.
Add a confidence score alongside the category, so downstream code can discard the low-confidence labels.
Drop the enum and let category be free text, so the model can describe what it actually sees in the document.
Keep the enum and add a prompt line telling the model not to guess when the category is genuinely ambiguous.

exp: A strict enum with no honest escape leaves guessing as the only way to satisfy the schema, so an "unclear" value gives ambiguity somewhere to go. A confidence score is the strongest alternative and does let downstream code filter — but the label itself is still a guess, and the record still asserts a category it does not have.

q: You process 10,000 documents nightly through the Message Batches API. A handful fail. How do you re-run only those without reprocessing the successful ones?

choices.t: Correlate requests and results by custom_id, then submit a new batch containing only the failed identifiers.
Rely on the results arriving in request order, and resubmit the entries at the positions that failed.
Resubmit the whole batch, since reprocessing the successful documents costs less than tracking failures.
Move the failed documents to the synchronous API individually, since a batch cannot target a subset.

exp: custom_id ties a result back to the request that produced it, so the failures are identifiable and a second batch can contain only them. Relying on result order is the strongest alternative and is the intuition custom_id exists to replace — batch results are not guaranteed to come back in submission order.
